News.title: 'Exhausted' new mum, 18, wakes to find days-old baby dead in her arms
News.content:
'Exhausted' new mum, 18, wakes to find days-old baby dead in her arms

Lydia Pass, 18, found her five-day-old daughter Arabella Mayer unresponsive in her arms after falling asleep with the baby while sitting in a chair, an inquest heard

View 4 Images Arabella Mayer with mum Lydia Pass (Image: Stoke Sentinel)

A young mum was left distraught after waking up to find her five-day old baby lifeless in her arms.

‌



Lydia Pass, 18, found little Arabella Mayer unresponsive in the early hours of June 17 after falling asleep with the baby while sitting in a chair, an inquest heard.

‌



Arabella was born less than a week earlier at the Royal Stoke University Hospital on June 12. The newborn was taken back to the family's home in Abbey Hulton, Stoke-on-Trent, shortly afterwards.

‌



Lydia and her partner Ryan, 18, had gone to bed at around midnight after feeding Arabella and putting her to sleep. The pair were woken at 3am to Arabella crying, before they changed and fed her, and returned to bed.

But Lydia awoke sitting in a chair at 5.45am with Arabella lying unresponsive in her arms. The distraught young mum had no recollection of picking Arabella up or falling back asleep, reports The Sentinel.

View 4 Images Arabella with parents 18-year-old Lydia Pass and Ryan Mayer (Image: Stoke Sentinel)

‌



An inquest heard Lydia may have been suffering with anaemia-related exhaustion following her traumatic three-day birth, during which she "lost pints of blood".

Lydia immediately sought help after discovering Arabella had stopped breathing. Her brother called 999 and began performing CPR until paramedics arrived.

Arabella was rushed to the Royal Stoke, where medics managed to revive her heartbeat, but she had already been "clinically dead" for around 50 minutes.

‌



Dr Sukesh Mohta, a consultant at Royal Stoke's paediatric intensive care unit, oversaw Arabella's care.

He told the inquest: "The brain can only survive for around four or five minutes without oxygen. Anything longer than that is seriously concerning. Through CPR, we can try to maintain some kind of blood flow, but it's nowhere near as effective as the heart pumping.

"Our first action was simply to prevent further injury. We employed neuro-protection. This involved placing her into an artificial coma to protect her brain. Then the hope is to take her off the support. But when we performed a brain scan the results were very poor.

‌



View 4 Images Arabella was found unresponsive in the early hours of June 17

"We had multiple difficult discussions with the family. It became clear that the situation was not survivable. The decision was made to withdraw life support on June 20."

Paediatric Pathologist Marta Cohen suggested that Arabella could have asphyxiated either due to an undiagnosed genetic problem or because of the way she fell asleep.

‌



She said: "We don't know why she collapsed. Sudden unexpected death happens in infants under one year of age. It is where death is unexplained. It is very rare in children who are only a few days old."

Detective Inspector Adam Goodyer, of Staffordshire Police's child protective services, ruled out any suggestion of neglect.

He said: "In my conclusion, it's a very sad tragedy. Her exhausted mum had picked her up in the night to settle her and then fallen asleep with Arabella in her arms. There are no neglect issues here. She was very well cared for in a loving family. I extend my sincere condolences to them all."

‌



View 4 Images The baby was born at Royal Stoke University Hospital (Image: Pete Stonier / Stoke Sentinel)

Coroner Lindsey Tonks recorded that Arabella suffered a delayed sudden death in the context of unsafe sleeping.

Ms Tonks concluded: "Here we have two parents and an extended family who had got everything ready for their newborn. They had set up a lovely home for her to return to after a particularly difficult labour and birth. There were no health concerns in those first five days.

Article continues below

"The birth had taken a lot out of Arabella's mum. That and the challenge of being a new mum had left her exhausted. She awoke to find Arabella unresponsive in her arms with no idea how she came to be there. Her mum did everything she could. Her family did everything they could to give her the best chance at survival.

"There was no evidence of anything being done intentionally or any indication of neglect. The police were very clear on that. The medical team were also very clear on that. I hope that can reassure the mum. There is no suggestion that she has done anything wrong.

"It is clear that this was a mum who had done all she could to try to provide a loving home for her daughter. This was a terribly tragic situation that no parent would ever want to experience. All I can do is offer my most sincere condolences to the family. This is a situation nobody ever wants to face. This was just a terrible, terrible tragedy."

News.title: Mum who spent life savings on lipo and breast augmentation dies during operation
News.content:
Mum who spent life savings on lipo and breast augmentation dies during operation

Sara Milena Echeverría Alcendra spent her family's savings on liposuction and breast augmentation surgery, but tragically died while at the clinic in Colombia

View 3 Images Sara Milena Echeverría Alcendra spent months preparing for the surgery (Image: Jam Press)

A mother has died during cosmetic surgery after spending her family's life savings on the procedure.

‌



Sara Milena Echeverría Alcendra spent around five months preparing for liposuction and breast augmentation after losing 4st 8lbs in a bid to qualify for the operation. But just hours after entering the operating theatre at a cosmetic clinic in Colombia, the 31-year-old suffered a fatal medical emergency.

‌



Her devastated husband, Carlos Hernández, is now demanding answers, insisting his wife was healthy and had passed every pre-operative medical test.

‌



Authorities in Barranquilla have launched an investigation into her death, to determine whether it was the result of an unforeseeable medical complication or medical negligence.

View 3 Images Authorities have launched an investigation into her death (Image: Jam Press)

Teens forced to stop people recording West Mersea beach tragedy as girl and woman died READ MORE :

UK weather maps show 40C heatwave within days as 18 counties hit 39C or more READ MORE :

According to Mr Hernández, the couple had saved for years to pay for the operation, which ultimately cost more than £15,000 (65.3 million Colombian pesos). “That was my savings. It's almost half a lifetime,” he said.

‌



Sara, a shopkeeper who worked alongside her husband, had originally weighed around 15st 7lbs before being told by her surgeon she needed to lose weight before undergoing cosmetic surgery. Mr Hernández said she then embarked on a strict five-month programme involving a nutritionist, diet and exercise, eventually losing 4st 8lbs.

“She had the surgery in mind because she weighed 100 kilos, but the doctor told her she first had to lose weight,” he said. “She lost more than 30 kilos. Then she underwent a series of examinations to check she was suitable and everything came back very well.”

The family said Sara underwent extensive pre-surgical testing and was also prescribed treatment to increase her haemoglobin levels before being cleared for surgery. The procedure was scheduled to take place at the Diamanti Aesthetic Clinic in Barranquilla.

‌



According to Mr Hernández, they arrived at the clinic at around 7.30am and the surgeon told him shortly before 11am that Sara was being taken into theatre. The operation was expected to last around seven hours.

Instead, just over two hours after surgery began, Mr Hernández received devastating news. The grieving husband said he has still not been given a clear explanation for what happened.

View 3 Images Sara with her husband, Carlos (Image: Jam Press)

‌



"I want everything that happened to my wife to be clarified because she was a healthy, young woman," he said. "They haven't told me anything. I asked the doctor when I went in to see her and he just opened his hands as if he didn't know what had happened."

Mr Hernández said the only person who attempted to explain the situation was the anaesthetist, but he struggled to understand the medical explanation while overwhelmed with grief. "He explained something to me that I didn't understand," he said. "Why would I say I understood when I didn't, especially in my pain?"

Sara's father, Roicer Echeverría, also questioned the circumstances surrounding his daughter's death. He claimed the family had initially been told the procedure had not yet begun when she suffered cardiac arrest.

‌



However, after seeing her body, he believed surgery had already taken place. "If all the tests were fine, what right do they have to say my daughter suddenly became ill?" he said.

“We had been told they hadn't even started the procedure when she went into cardiac arrest. We were left with doubts. We went to see her and removed the sheet. We saw she had indeed undergone a procedure.”

The total bill reportedly exceeded the original agreed price after additional charges were added for treatment including hernia repair, a post-operative pain pump and medical insurance.

‌



Despite choosing what they believed was a reputable, licensed clinic rather than an unregulated provider, the family now wants investigators to determine whether mistakes were made during the operation.

Following Sara's death, the clinic reportedly published documents on social media showing the permits issued by Colombia's health authorities allowing it to perform cosmetic surgery. No public statement explaining the circumstances of her death has been released.

Sara leaves behind her husband and the couple's two children, aged 12 and eight.

Article continues below

Her body has been transferred to forensic specialists for a post-mortem examination, with prosecutors now investigating the exact cause of her death and whether any criminal or professional liability exists.

News.title: How the mystery of dead animals dumped in villages led to a hidden world of illegal hunts
News.content:
On a remote Cambridgeshire farm, where his nearest neighbour is half a mile away, Mathew Latta was making lunch when the peace was shattered by the sound of loud exhausts.

Latta ran to the window to see a convoy of more than a dozen 4x4s heading towards his farm. His iron gates were cut open with an angle grinder and concrete blocks were shifted out of the way to clear the convoy's path.

The vehicles drove right over his fields at speed, tearing up the crops and skirting the fence by the family's garden. Then more than 70 people got out of the vehicles, men dressed in military fatigues and balaclavas, cheering and playing music.

Dogs were brought out on leads and began to hunt hares.

"They were all stood up on their cars with binoculars," says Latta. "I would say this is 100% a properly organised coursing event, with competitors and competitive dogs. People watching the course - and watching and betting on that sport. It was quite terrifying."

Warning: This story contains images of dead animals

Latta and his family were trapped in their home. They kept calling the police, but nobody came. His daughter, then aged seven, was terrified and kept asking: "Are these men gonna come inside, daddy?"

More than three hours later, the bloodsport was finally over and the crowd dispersed. They left behind four cars, one of them a burnt-out wreck. It emerged that, earlier that day, the convoy had rampaged through an area 20 miles (32km) long in the county, forcing other cars off the road and even robbing a petrol station.

News.title: Trump takes swipes at press during White House Correspondents' Dinner
News.content:
US President Donald Trump has taken swipes at the media at the White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) dinner, a night that celebrated press freedom after the first event was cancelled by a shooting three months ago.

The president sat as reporters from outlets he has sparred with and even sued, including the New York Times, CNN and the Wall Street Journal, came up to be honoured with awards.

The outgoing WHCA head said she would "refuse to let an act of violence have the final word", referring to the gunman tackled at the first dinner in April.

But the tone shifted as Trump aimed barbs at the "fake news" and accused many journalists in the room of having "Trump Derangement Syndrome".

In her remarks, WHCA President Weijia Jiang of CBS News said the event would return to the scene of the April shooting, the Washington Hilton, next year.

The officer shot at the scene, officer Victor Gonzalez of the US Secret Service, was given an award by Trump for his actions on the night of the shooting.

Trump stood and shook hands with award winners, including a Wall Street Journal team who was given an award for coverage of Trump's links to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.

Ahead of the event, many in the White House press corps theorised that Trump - who often criticises many of the reporters seated just metres away in the room - would deliver a stern rebuke of the media.

News.title: Police declare 'major incident' as wind change increases Cairngorms wildfire risk
News.content:
A major incident has been declared by Police Scotland as emergency services continue to tackle a wildfire which has been burning in the Cairngorms National Park for 10 days.

The force said it followed "a significant change in weather conditions" which has increased the risk of fire spreading towards the village of Nethy Bridge.

All Nethy Bridge residents have been evacuated as a precaution to allow emergency services to continue their response.

But a local resident told the BBC the wildfire should have been declared a major incident sooner and the lack of communication from authorities had been "pretty poor".

The BBC has contacted the Scottish government and Police Scotland for comment.

First Minister John Swinney, who held a meeting of the Scottish government's resilience room early on Saturday, said additional police resources were being deployed to assist with the Nethy Bridge evacuation.

He urged people to "respect the exclusion zone that's been put in place", adding that the change in weather conditions illustrated "the scale and difficulty of the situation that we are managing".

Smoke from the wildfire can now be seen 59 miles away in Aberdeen following a change in wind direction.

Supt Judy Hill said weather conditions "experienced within the Cairngorms over the last 24 hours have added further complexities to this situation".

"With evidence suggesting the fire is spreading towards Nethy Bridge, the decision has been taken to declare a major incident and evacuate residents as a precaution."

She said additional police resources were being deployed to help contact those who need to leave their properties.

News.title: Horror injury overshadows gymnastics silver for England at Commonwealths
News.content:
A sickening injury to England's Gabriel Langton overshadowed his team's silver medal in the men's team gymnastics final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

The 19-year-old, from the City of Birmingham Gymnastics Club, needed lengthy treatment on the mat after a horrible fall in the final rotation of the evening at The Arena.

Langton fell head first to the floor after missing his catch on the horizontal metal bar, three metres in the air, leading to a lengthy delay to the action as he was tended to by up to a dozen medical staff.

He was eventually led away on a trolley after being moved on to a stretcher with his head and neck braced and left to huge applause from the packed crowd who had spent much of the previous 10 minutes in hushed silence.

Langton was seen to be conscious and moving his legs and arms before leaving the arena floor, while team officials later said he was moving and speaking to doctors.

In a statement, Team England said: "We are grateful to the medical teams who responded immediately to provide assistance.

"He has been taken to hospital and we will share more information when it is available."

When competition resumed, his England team-mates were unable to overhaul their deficit to Canada who claimed their first gold medal in the event in 20 years, having finished second to England at the past two games.

Langton, a late call-up to Team England in the place of the injured six-time Olympic medallist Max Whitlock, was unable to join his teammates on the podium as England collected their silver medals.

Team-mate Luke Whitehouse, who was first on to the apparatus after the competition restarted and posted a relatively low score of 11.700, said: "When something like that happens, you've just got to forget about it and reset. I just had to focus on my routine one skill at a time."

Whitehouse added: "From what we've heard, he's doing OK. Gymnastics is such a dangerous sport and things like this remind us of that. It's one of those things you have to put out of your mind."

Felix Dolci, who helped Canada to gold and led qualifying for the all-around competition, said: "It's terrible but it goes to show that gymnastics is a very, very difficult and complicated sport. It's dangerous you know sometimes.

"All our thoughts go to Gabriel and the team. Pushing through this is definitely not easy, England stayed focussed, they stayed in the zone, a huge shout out to them because that's not an easy one.

"For any gymnast that was on the field of play, seeing this not only is difficult, but something you never want to see. It goes to show how hard the sport is."

Hamish Carter from Team Scotland - who narrowly missed out on a bronze medal to Australia in the final rotation - said: "I didn't actually see what happened. I'm just so happy that he's alright and, having experienced that, anything could have happened.

"We've walked away with no medal but I'm thinking of Gabe in this moment."

News.title: ADHD has rewired the workplace. This is what it means for bosses and workers
News.content:
Taking one of the UK's biggest grocery chains to an employment tribunal was something that Ryan Toghill says almost took over his life.

"It was all I could think about for 18 months and more," he says.

The deputy store manager at Lidl, who'd told his bosses he'd been diagnosed with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), was called to a disciplinary meeting after breaking company rules by using equipment he hadn't been trained to use. After that meeting, Ryan was dismissed for gross misconduct.

He successfully appealed the decision and was offered a lower-paid role. He rejected it and took his case to a tribunal. Eventually, he was awarded more than Â£45,000 when the judge found his former employer hadn't fully taken his ADHD diagnosis into account during the disciplinary process.

The judgement found reasonable adjustments during the process hadn't been offered to him, such as additional breaks.

He'd been described by a manager as showing "a lack of remorse," something the tribunal found was clearly linked with his communication differences associated with having ADHD.

"I don't show a lot of emotions," Ryan explains. "I could be incredibly happy, angry, upset, or remorseful, and my facial expressions and tone of voice would essentially remain the same."

The tribunal upheld part of his claims for unfair dismissal, wrongful dismissal and a failure to make reasonable adjustments. Lidl says it's "committed to ensuring that everyone receives the reasonable adjustments, clear communication and support they need to thrive."

Campaigners, lawyers and HR teams say cases like this highlight a shift that businesses should be paying attention to.

Thousands of people have been diagnosed as neurodivergent in the last few years, an umbrella term that covers autism, ADHD and other conditions such as dyslexia and Tourette's syndrome.

Since the pandemic in particular, diagnosis rates for ADHD and autism have been rising, and they're featuring more regularly in disputes in employment tribunals.

News.title: The pop band who went from playing for rescue dogs to selling out arenas
News.content:
Every band has to earn its stripes. Some have it harder than others.

At AC/DC's first gig, the club owner cut the power because they were too noisy. Sam Smith started at barn dances, singing on top of a haystack. At Robert Smith's first concert, he got so drunk that he sang David Bowie's Suffragette City while the rest of the band played Jimi Hendrix's Foxy Lady.

But LA pop trio Muna can top them all.

At the start of their career, the band got a call from their record label. We know you've just flown overnight from London, they said, but you have to get to Las Vegas.

Why? Because they'd been booked to play Pet-A-Palooza, a dog adoption festival sponsored by the local radio station. If they turned up, the station would support their new single.

"We were all sick, so it was doomed from the start," recalls guitarist Josette Maskin.

"It was an acoustic set, but we didn't have a sound guy, and the guitar started feeding back."

The noise, according to singer Katie Gavin, was like an unholy screech.

"The dogs were getting upset," says Maskin, wincing at the memory. "They just howled the whole time.

"We were mortified, but looking back, it is so funny. And I've gotten to share those experiences with some of my best friends, and that's what life is really about."

News.title: Long overdue, life-changing or frivolous? Your thoughts on wedding rule changes
News.content:
The day Sam and Courtney Scholey became husband and wife didn't feel like their wedding day.

There was no walking down the aisle, no rings exchanged, no wedding dress, and no music.

That all came several days later, when the pair had a bespoke ceremony led by a celebrant who knew them, at a venue in the Oxfordshire countryside. It was their dream wedding - but it wasn't legal in England and Wales.

And so in April, they forked out hundreds of pounds to quietly sign papers at a library in Buckingham.

"For us, that day was as insignificant as possible," Courtney told the BBC. "It was just the words we had to say to make it legally binding."

The Scholeys are one of a growing number of couples who feel the rigid rules around weddings are making getting married more stressful, more expensive and less meaningful.

But under new proposals announced this month - described by the government as the biggest shake-up of wedding laws in 200 years - couples in England and Wales could have the freedom to hold official marriage ceremonies in a wider array of unconventional locations, from forests to beaches, as long as the location is approved by a registered officiant.

It's welcome news for Nicky Brown, who said she wants to exchange vows in a wildly picturesque corner of Wales, with just her mum and her partner's mum as witnesses.

"I'd be quite happy to get married in a field full of sheep," the 57-year-old told the BBC.

But some say the sacred tradition of marriage is being perverted.

News.title: Claudia Winkleman's chat show ended after one series - can anyone replace Graham Norton?
News.content:
When Lisa Kudrow appeared on The Claudia Winkleman Show earlier this year, she was visibly delighted to meet Linda from The Traitors.

The Friends actress, probably the most famous guest the programme had during its seven-week run, said it was "thrilling" to meet one of the reality show's breakout stars, who she revealed had even inspired one of her own recent performances.

As host of The Traitors, Winkleman was ideally placed to introduce the pair, resulting in the kind of wonderfully bizarre meeting of minds normally seen on The Graham Norton Show.

But Winkleman's own chat show did not last long enough for any more unusual guest combinations on its teal sofa. The presenter quit last week after just one series, saying she was simply "too nervous to enjoy it".

It had made sense for the BBC to commission The Claudia Winkleman Show, given the presenter's popularity on programmes such as Strictly.

There's a different level of pressure, however, hosting a show with your own name above the door.

News.title: Huge explosion and fire rip through Essex industrial site
News.content:
People living near the fire - which happened close to the village of Rettendon, south of Chelmsford - were urged to keep their windows closed as smoke spread.

As of Friday evening, it was not clear whether there had been casualties, but in an update that night, Dave Bond of Essex County Fire and Rescue Service said: "While on the scene, fertiliser inside one of the units exploded and residents across the county have reported hearing and feeling it.

"This is why we declared a major incident, and I want to reassure our residents that there is no wider risk to the public at this time."

He said "everybody at the scene is safe" but that residents have been evacuated.

The fire service said the response was scaled down, with about 25 firefighters on scene as of 08:00 BST on Saturday as well as specialist officers and advisors to extinguish the rest of the blaze.

Crews are expected to remain on site for the rest of Saturday, and smoke is still coming from the scene, the fire service added.

East of England Ambulance Service said its hazardous area response team and the police were also in attendance.

Earlier on Friday evening, Bond said there was still "significant smoke" at the scene, but he believed that the fire had been "surrounded".

News.title: Teenage boy dies after stabbing in Luton as police launch murder investigation
News.content:
Police have launched a murder investigation after a teenage boy died following a stabbing in Luton.

Bedfordshire Police said officers responded to reports of violent disorder in Kingsway Recreation Ground at about 18:30 on Friday, where a number of teenagers were seen carrying large knives.

A 17-year-old, who has not been identified, was taken to hospital with multiple stab wounds but was pronounced dead shortly after, the force said.

One teenage boy has been arrested on suspicion of violent disorder and is in police custody for questioning. A second was arrested but remains in hospital with serious but non-life threatening injuries.

Police are appealing to the public for information.

In a statement, Det Ch Insp Nick Gardener condemned the "horrific violence" that has "sadly cost a teenage boy his life today".

"Our thoughts are first and foremost with the loved ones of the boy who lost his life in such tragic circumstances," he said.

Such incidents have "a significant impact on our communities", he said.

He also urged the public to contact police with any information they have and not to share any images and videos circulating on social media.

An increased police presence and patrols will remain in the area.

Zanib Raja, a councillor for the Biscot Ward in Luton, asked people not to share alleged videos of the incident online.

In a statement on Facebook, she said: "A tragic incident took place today in Kingsway Park, a place many of us grew up in, played in, and built memories in.

"A place that should be safe for families, children, and every resident of our town. Instead, a man lost his life in broad daylight. A family has been shattered. Luton is hurting."

Raja urged the community to come together.

News.title: Heatwave conditions to return for many as UK temperatures to peak at 35C
News.content:
For most of England and Wales the third heatwave of the year ended last weekend when cooler air arrived, dropping maximum temperatures widely to 20-24C.

However, two locations - Usk and Exeter - have continued to just reach their heatwave criteria since then and have now reached 20 consecutive days - the longest run so far this year.

As temperatures drop further over the weekend, and parts of the UK see a little rain, even these local heatwaves are likely to come to an end.

However, it may only be a temporary break.

Next week, high pressure is set to build close to the south of the UK meaning rain-bearing weather fronts will stall.

Any wet weather will become confined to northern and western areas - especially north-west Scotland - and in southern parts of the UK temperatures look set to climb once again.

This could well mean a fourth heatwave is on the cards - although according to the Met Office isolated high temperatures might not be enough.

They say that: "If only one or two stations reach heatwave criteria, that would not be defined as a heatwave."

News.title: It's the cocktail taking young drinkers by storm - but the packaging is 'unrecyclable'
News.content:
Cleaning up after pre-drinks, AÃ©dÃ©n Rooney puts his empty BuzzBallz in the recycling.

"It's plastic and metal, so I'd just assume it's recyclable," he said.

The company behind the bright, pre-mixed cocktails that have taken Gen Z by storm said they were recyclable on its website, but experts say this is not true.

BuzzBallz cannot be recycled as the PET plastic ball cannot be separated from the aluminium lid, global environmental action body WRAP said.

"It's greenwashing. I'm shocked," AÃ©dÃ©n said.

BuzzBallz blamed a website error for claiming they were recyclable via Terracycle, a US-only scheme, but did not comment on its now-deleted FAQ that said they were recyclable where UK councils allow.

News.title: Law student is charged over intercepted bomb in car
News.content:
A 25-year-old law student has appeared in court charged over a bomb which was discovered in a car in the Republic of Ireland.

Isobella Perrie Sullivan, from Abbeylands Park in Clane, County Kildare, was charged with the possession of explosives.

It was alleged she was driving the car which was intercepted by gardaÃ­ (Irish police) near Carrickmacross, County Monaghan, on Wednesday.

A defence solicitor told the court his client had been asked to take a bag to Northern Ireland and had not been aware what was in it.

Earlier on Friday, gardaÃ­ told reporters their interception was part of an operation targeting dissident republican activity.

The accused, who was arrested on Wednesday, was brought before a special sitting of Trim District Court in County Meath on Friday evening.

A member of the Garda Special Detective Unit told the court the car she was driving was stopped by officers on N2 at Aclint, south of Carrickmacross.

News.title: Man describes trying to save mother and daughter who drowned off Essex beach
News.content:
A day-tripper has told the BBC how he dived into the sea in an attempt to save a mother and daughter who drowned off an Essex beach.

Craig Bowe, 42, battled the incoming tide at West Mersea, near Colchester, three times after hearing screams on Wednesday evening.

The kitchen fitter, who was on a day trip from Hertfordshire to celebrate his daughter's 10th birthday, managed to haul Shally and Samiha Rahman from the waves and also helped a seven-year-old boy onto a lifeboat.

Despite his efforts, the pair - aged 41 and 15 - died in the desperate attempt to bring the boy to shore.

The boy, who became stranded during a family day out from Barking, east London, was airlifted to hospital and remained there in a critical condition on Friday.

Three others were taken by ambulance to another hospital after the incident unfolded at about 17:35 BST.

News.title: Officers hurt as police boat hits Westminster Bridge
News.content:
Five Metropolitan Police officers have been injured after a police boat struck Westminster Bridge in central London.

The Met said the incident occurred at about 15:40 BST and involved a boat from the Marine Policing Unit which was carrying armed officers.

One officer has since been discharged from hospital and the others have serious but non-life-threatening injuries.

The police confirmed that no members of the public were involved or injured in the crash.

The police boat was responding to a report of a person in the water near Battersea.

The Met said in a statement: "As a result of the collision, three officers were thrown from the boat into the water. They were recovered by those on nearby boats.

"Additional officers responded alongside the London Ambulance Service and London Fire Brigade."

The Met's Cmdr Nick John thanked river users "who came to the aid of the officers, as well as other police and emergency service colleagues who immediately made their way to the scene to assist".

He added: "The quick-thinking and professionalism of all those involved undoubtedly prevented any further injuries."

News.title: Angela Rayner rules out rent controls in England
News.content:
Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has said Prime Minister Andy Burnham is not looking at bringing in rent controls in England.

She told BBC Breakfast that changes made through the Renters' Rights Act, which came into effect in May, were "already having a significant impact on the market".

She added that controls which had been implemented in some areas of the UK over the past few years had not "necessarily brought rents down".

In 2023 when he was the mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham called for freezes to private sector rents until the cost of living crisis was over.

But Rayner told the BBC on Friday: "I don't think that rent freezes, rent controls, is a way forward at the moment.

"Three years ago, Andy called for that because there was a significant crisis in the rental market.

"We implemented between then the Renters' Rights Act which is giving renters more power and control."

Temporary rent controls were introduced in Scotland in October 2022 but expired last year.

Under new legislation, ministers in Holyrood will be able to designate certain places in Scotland as rent control areas - expected to come in by 2027.

Councils will be able to cap rent increases on some properties at a maximum of 6%.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski has said he wants to see rent controls brought in for all rented property in England.

Responding to Rayner's interview, he described Burnham as "continuity Starmer", posting on X: "The new prime minister talks a lot of about helping with the cost of living crisis. This is the one single measure that would help the most and save billions. All talk."

Jeremy Corbyn, who pledged to bring in rent controls during the 2019 general election when he was the Labour leader, described Rayner's announcement as "extremely disappointing".

"There is no hope of ending homelessness if we do not stand up to vested interests and take action against extortionate private rents.

"We need rent controls, and we need them now."

Sir Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, has also long called on the government to implement a cap.

But Gareth Bacon, the Conservative's shadow housing minister, said rent controls would be "disastrous" and "intensify the damage done by Labour's agenda that has driven landlords from the market and reduced choice for renters".

"Labour are clearly divided. Burnham's pick for housing secretary has disowned a policy he himself has repeatedly backed," he said.

The term rent controls describes a range of measures a government can implement - from capping price increases to freezing them for a period of time.

Landlord groups say they may exacerbate the housing crisis by putting owners off renting out property.

The Renters' Rights Act was brought in to give more stability and security to the 11 million people who rent from private landlords.

Under the legislation, fixed-term tenancies have been banned and it is now significantly harder for landlords to evict tenants.

Rents can also only be increased once a year to the property's "open market rent".

News.title: Horses run from thick black smoke as wildfires rage in France
News.content:
Video circulating on social media shows horses fleeing thick black smoke as wildfires continue to rage in southwest France.

Officials have ordered the evacuation of large parts of Bordeaux’s suburbs, including the areas of Le Haillan, Eysines ​and Merignac.

“The fires ‌which are hitting our country have reached a level that has never ​been seen before,” French ‌prime minister Sebastien Lecornu wrote on X on Saturday.

The French army has also been drafted in to help with the crisis as the blaze showed no signs of slowing down.

French officials warned that winds were likely to exacerbate the fires.

India’s education minister Dharmendra Pradhan has resigned after weeks of youth-led protests demanding that he take responsibility for an examination paper leak that affected millions of students.

The move marked the first major concession from prime minister Narendra Modi’s government after a movement led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) resulted in weeks of nationwide demonstrations, sit-ins, and hunger strikes demanding Mr Pradhan’s resignation.

The CJP sprung up as a satirical platform, providing a rallying point for millions of young Indians frustrated over high unemployment and exam paper leaks and seeking greater government accountability.

Over the past week, tens of thousands gathered in the capital of Delhi demanding the resignation of Mr Pradhan ⁠over leaks of the medical entrance test paper that affected some two million students ​in ⁠May and have been linked to several student suicides.

The demonstrations have become one of the most visible signs of public dissent against Mr Modi’s government in recent years, with thousands returning to the streets even after police used tear gas and batons this week to disperse marchers trying to reach parliament.

open image in gallery India's education minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigns after protest across the country over paper leaks ( AFP/Getty )

The resignation handed a major victory to the protesters nationwide who demanded that Mr Pradhan take responsibility for the leak of National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET), India's undergraduate medical school entrance exam.

The “cockroaches”, as the protesters call themselves, welcomed the move.

“This is democracy. He has resigned,” said Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of CJP, who started it as a mocking response to a pointed comment from India’s top judge, Justice Surya Kant, who likened India's unemployed youth in a speech to "cockroaches".

“We have two more demands. We won't go like this. Dharmendra Pradhan has resigned. But the families of the children who committed suicide should receive compensation of one crore rupees (£77,700). They should get it. One crore rupees compensation to all those families. And second, these police goons who acted on the 20th (July). Action must be taken against the police officers for that. Remember, do not mess with cockroach.”

Mr Pradhan’s resignation came even as police fired ⁠tear gas to scatter young protesters in the Indian capital, hours before their leaders were set ‌to hold another round ​of talks ‌with ministers ⁠to push for ⁠the move.

open image in gallery Supporters of India's Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) hold signs during the ongoing protests, a few days after thousands of protesters marched towards parliament demanding the resignation ( Reuters )

"Considering the situation that has arisen at Jantar Mantar and across the country, so that anti-national forces do not take advantage of this situation ... I have sent my resignation letter to the Prime Minister," Mr Pradhan wrote in his post.

"I deeply respect the aspirations, feelings, and legitimate expectations of the country's youth."

Cheers erupted among the thousands of protesters who have been rallying in central Delhi and elsewhere as the news spread.

open image in gallery Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) supporters celebrate the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi on 25 July 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

The government has shut down the exit of 18 metro stations closer to the protest site and suspended the internet in the area, in a bid to contain it.

Anger had boiled over since police on Monday injured many students, launching baton charges, and firing tear gas to deter crowds of protesters marching on parliament.

open image in gallery Supporters of India's Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) queue up for free pizza sent by unknown supporters through food delivery apps ( Reuters )

The protests, led largely by ⁠young people and triggered by discontent over leaks of question papers ‌for high-stakes entrance ​exams, reflect anger over ‌job scarcity, corruption and government ​accountability.

Rick Moranis received a warm welcome at his Comic-Con debut following decades out of the spotlight.

The 73-year-old joined a panel event on Friday 24 July to promote Spaceballs: The New One, a forthcoming sequel to the 1987 Mel Brooks Star Wars parody.

He was met with a standing ovation from fans – and an on-stage bow from his co-stars, including Josh Gad, Keke Palmer, Lewis Pullman, and Daphne Zuniga.

“You made our childhoods better,” said moderator Kevin Smith as fans chanted: “Rick! Rick! Rick!”

Moranis rose to fame on the Canadian sketch show SCTV in 1980 after which he went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Eighties cinema, starring in films such as Streets of Fire (1983), Ghostbusters (1984), Little Shop of Horrors (1986) Spaceballs (1987), and Ghostbusters II (1989), Honey, I Shrunk the Kids (1989), My Blue Heaven (1990) and The Flintstones (1994).

He stepped away from live-action acting in 1997 in order to focus on raising his two children after his wife, Ann, died from breast cancer. Moranis has been largely absent from films and TV for most of this century, taking on voice acting roles instead.

In a rare interview back in 2015, Moranis raised the possibility of stepping back in front of the camera given that his children were grown up – but noted that he remains very “picky” about which roles he would accept. For example, he had no interest in returning for the 2024 Ghostbusters sequel despite the involvement of other original stars like Bill Murray.

The right opportunity arose with Spaceballs: The New One, which will see Moranis reprise his role as villain Dark Helmet.

open image in gallery Rick Moranis ( AP1994 )

Amazon MGM Studios officially announced that the actor would star in the highly anticipated sequel back in September following reports earlier that year.

It marks a major return to screen for Moranis, who said at the event: “The truth is that I had to say yes to this thing. It was the only way I could get Josh Gad to stop texting me. Actually, I started talking to Mel [Brooks] about the sequel in 1989. We kept talking about it.”

He joked: “I really wasn’t retired; I was just negotiating.”

Moranis added: “But no, this came along right at the right time, and I started talking to these folks and hearing who was going to be in it. I spoke to Josh Greenbaum and I heard that Bill Pullman was coming back and that [his son] Lewis was going to be in it too, and it just felt like this is it. It’s time and – yes. I said yes, and it is the best decision I’ve ever made.”

Pullman, who played the Han Solo parody character Lone Starr in the original comedy, will appear in the new film alongside his 33-year-old son Lewis. Meanwhile, Brooks is set to reprise his role as Yogurt, a parody of Yoda.

open image in gallery Rick Moranis is met with applause on stage at Comic-Con in 2026 ( Getty )

Neither Pullman, 72, and Brooks, who turned 100 in June, were present at the panel but both sent video messages to be shown to fans.

Moranis said that he had not seen Brooks in person in nearly four decades before they began work on the sequel. “I just kept getting phone calls from him every time another Star Wars would come out, and he would say, ‘We have to make the sequel. We have to make the sequel,’” Moranis said.

“When this finally happened, I came out to Los Angeles, went over to his house for the first time in 39 years.”

Spaceballs 2 is scheduled for release in 2027.

News.content:

It’s better to keep your mouth shut and appear stupid than to open it and remove all doubt,” my daughter Monica said, quoting a phrase often attributed to Mark Twain, as we stepped into the great novelist’s wonderfully eccentric Connecticut home on the second day of our father-daughter road trip through New England.

We had collected a black Subaru Forester from JFK airport and set off on an unusual 2,000-mile pilgrimage through the literary heart of New England. The idea was simple enough: visit the homes of America’s greatest writers, trace the landscapes that shaped them, and see whether genius leaves any trace in the places it once inhabited. It also doubled as a search for good food and long, uninterrupted conversations on the open road.

Mark Twain’s Hartford house is unlike any literary shrine. It looks as though a Mississippi steamboat has collided with a Victorian Gothic mansion and then been left to settle into something exuberantly American. Red brick, ornate chimneys and playful gables give it the air of a building that refuses to take itself too seriously.

open image in gallery Mark Twain’s house is defined by its red brick, ornate chimneys and playful gables ( Adams & Knight )

Inside, the guide referred to him exclusively as “Sam”, as though Samuel Clemens had simply stepped out for a moment. Monica happily discussed Huckleberry Finn while I quietly realised how much I had forgotten. Parents are supposed to know more than their children. Literary pilgrimages have a way of correcting such assumptions.

The house, built with the fortune of Twain’s heiress wife Olivia, was one of the first in America to have electricity and central heating. In 1881 they commissioned Louis Comfort Tiffany to transform the interiors into a theatrical blaze of embossed wallpaper, stencilled ceilings and deep reds and golds. It was spectacularly expensive and eventually helped drive Twain back onto the lecture circuit to repair the family finances.

Just a short walk away stands the more modest home of Harriet Beecher Stowe, author of Uncle Tom’s Cabin. It is hard to imagine a more concentrated patch of American literary history. In the billiard room upstairs, Twain wrote much of Huckleberry Finn, the novel often described as the foundation of modern American literature. Standing there, it was impossible not to see his journey – from riverboat pilot and penniless journalist to national figure – as a version of the American dream itself.

That first stop set the tone for everything that followed.

Over the next fortnight we crossed much of New England, tracing the lives of Herman Melville, Emily Dickinson, Louisa May Alcott, Edith Wharton, and the transcendentalists Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau. Between them came bass fishing, canoeing, long glacial lakes, strawberry fields, village greens and white-steepled churches. And everywhere, inevitably, lobster rolls and clam chowder.

The journey had been inspired partly by cinema. Paper Moon and On Golden Pond had long suggested that travel matters as much as arrival. (Fans of On Golden Pond should stay at the Von Horn Estate, which is a country house hotel actually on the lake.) Our version was considerably calmer. The only recurring dispute was musical. I leaned towards Pink Floyd; Monica introduced Geese, whom she described as “the modern Bob Dylan”. We found as much agreement over books as playlists as we juggled from the Grateful Dead to Oasis.

open image in gallery Long hours in the car created a space for family conversations that ordinary life rarely allows ( The Independent )

As the miles accumulated, something subtle shifted. Long hours in the car created a space for conversation that ordinary life rarely allows. Books gave way to politics, music, careers and the strange pleasure of simply observing America unfold beyond the windscreen. New England itself became part of the dialogue: maple forests blazing green, empty highways, and towns where white clapboard houses still gathered around village greens as though time had paused.

New England contains both astonishing beauty and an extraordinary density of history. Here, the first shots of the American Revolution were fired. Here, a young nation began to imagine itself. Here, writers would later find the landscapes that defined its literature. We stayed in a treehouse at The Winvian, a Connecticut country estate of cottages and seasonal delicacies in their restaurant. There were warnings to look out for wild bears, but the more obvious reality was charming bike rides in the nearby woods. Hotels are part of the American dream.

By the time we left Hartford, the purpose of the journey had already begun to shift. We had set out in search of writers’ houses. What we were discovering instead was something less tangible but more enduring: the pleasure of uninterrupted time together, measured in miles rather than minutes.

open image in gallery The treehouse accommodation at at The Winvian in Connecticut ( The Independent )



In the Berkshires, Herman Melville’s house at Arrowhead sits quietly beneath the shadow of Mount Greylock. It is modest, almost understated, and all the more powerful for it. Here Moby Dick was written – an epic that failed on publication and would not find its audience for decades.

Looking out across the landscape, it was easy to imagine Melville wrestling with his creation while the world outside remained indifferent. Every literary house seemed to carry the same lesson: recognition and talent rarely arrive at the same time. A wonderful diversion from the driver’s seat was staying at Prospect Berkshires on a lake with super stylish cabins and sauna huts, a zeitgeisty resort which leans into its stunning waterscape.

In Amherst, Emily Dickinson’s house offers a different kind of intensity. Small rooms, restrained light and a life deliberately narrowed to allow imagination to expand. She published almost nothing in her lifetime, yet her poetry now feels foundational to modern literature.

open image in gallery Emily Dickinson’s house has small rooms and restrained light ( Lynne Graves Photography )

A short drive away, Louisa May Alcott’s Orchard House tells another story entirely – one of family, imagination and quiet radicalism. Little Women was written here, drawing directly on domestic life yet reshaping it into something far more enduring. If Dickinson represents solitude, Alcott represents connection.

At Concord, Emerson and Thoreau’s world feels more conceptual than domestic. Walden Pond, in particular, where Thoreau lived in a wood hut for two years, two months and two days, resists cliche. It is smaller than expected, quieter, more ordinary – and yet it remains one of the most influential landscapes in American thought.

Here, nature was not scenery but philosophy. Simplicity was not aesthetic but moral. Walking the shoreline, it was easy to see how a new relationship between people and the natural world was once imagined here.

Between these lit-stops, New England revealed itself in less formal ways. Diners with creaking porches served eggs, hash browns and endless coffee. Coastal towns offered lobster rolls eaten at picnic tables overlooking grey Atlantic water. Lakes stretched long and still beneath impossible skies.

open image in gallery New England revealed itself to be at the forefront of Americana ( The Independent )

Standouts in New Haven, Connecticut, were sessional family pizza restaurant Modern Apizza and an ocean-side seafood restaurant Shell and Bones, which has true piquancy and zest for utterly delicious seafood. Do not pass on the oysters. Another stunning food high spot was Woods Hill Table, a perfect local restaurant in Lexington, Massachusetts, with a sophisticated vibe.

New England has always been, we reminded ourselves, at the forefront of Americana: Jaws, The Stepford Wives, Nathaniel Hawthorne’s The Scarlet Letter and Arlo Guthrie’s plaintive anti-Vietnam tour de force “Alice’s Restaurant”.

At Lexington, Massachusetts, history becomes physical. On the village green where the first shots of the American Revolution were fired, Gerry Marrocco, a charismatic guide in period costume, recounted Paul Revere’s midnight ride, warning “the Brits are coming” with evangelical precision. It is easy to forget how recent this history is.

open image in gallery Guide Gerry Marrocco recounts Paul Revere’s midnight ride ( The Independent )

We stayed at the Inn at Hastings Park in Lexington, Massachusetts, which has been converted by its perfectionist owner Trisha Keneally to be a beacon of high American cuisine. It is on the old Boston coach road and worth any diversion.

Nearby, architecture tells a different story of reinvention. The Bauhaus-inspired house designed by Walter Gropius in Massachusetts feels like a clean break from the past – precise, modern, almost radical in its simplicity. New England is rarely one thing for long. Gropius’s house is enchanting and revolutionary.

Somewhere along these roads, another journey was taking place.

Monica and I shared driving, music and long stretches of silence punctuated by argument and laughter. We disagreed over playlists, agreed over food and slowly accumulated a shared map of references that belonged only to us.

The landscape itself seemed to encourage it. Maple-lined roads, sudden glimpses of lake, and towns with names that echoed American history – Concord, Salem, Lexington, New Haven – created a rhythm that made conversation inevitable. New ventures reflect the entrepreneurial as well as the indulgent.

The Lake Estate on Winnisquam is a £100m dream vacation spot created by Patty and Ed Rocco. It’s straight out of a Robert Redford idyll, Arcadian and ambitious. It seems to whisper from their side of the pond: eat your heart out, Lake Como. What began as a literary pilgrimage had become something else, a reminder that time together is not an incidental benefit of travel, but its real purpose.

open image in gallery The beautiful Lake Estate on Winnisquam ( The Lake Estate on Winnisquam )

By the end of 2,000 miles, we had visited writers who shaped a nation’s imagination and landscapes that shaped theirs. But the most lasting impression was not literary at all. It was the sense that journeys rarely deliver what they promise – and often deliver something better instead.

We set out to understand America through its greatest writers. We ended up understanding something simpler: that travel changes not only what you see, but how you talk to the person beside you. Twain believed that travel is fatal to prejudice. He might also have added that it is remarkably good for families.

How to do it

As Sir Keir Starmer’s premiership neared its end, an unassuming social club on the outskirts of a former mining town became the nerve centre for a reboot of the Labour Party.

The Stubshaw Cross Community Club at the north-east of Ashton-in-Makerfield was home to Andy Burnham’s by-election campaign at the start of the summer.

The choice of a traditional Labour club as his campaign headquarters illustrated what the then-mayor of Greater Manchester wished to achieve as he sought more than just the Makerfield seat.

It represented what would soon become his Labour Party getting back to its grassroots, reconnecting with voters who have traditionally been the core of its electoral coalition but abandoned it in their droves at the local elections just weeks before.

The club is a far cry from Islington’s now-lost Granita restaurant, where Tony Blair and Gordon Brown were said to have struck a gentleman’s agreement about leadership and set about rebuilding the Labour Party in their image in 1994.

“He does politics and he does symbolism very well”, Patrick Hurley, Labour MP for fellow North West constituency Southport, said of Mr Burnham’s campaign base.

open image in gallery Inside the Burnham campaign HQ at Stubshaw Cross Community and Sports Club in May ( Getty )

“Running the most consequential by-election campaign for the past 100 years out of the hatch of a Labour club in Lancashire – that just speaks volumes, and it speaks volumes to where the Labour Party goes next”, he told The Independent.

“It speaks volumes to the fact that under Andy, we've got our groove back a little bit. The people who we were set up as a political party and a movement to advocate for and to work on behalf of, I think they realise that.”

Mr Burnham used his first week in office to announce a series of policies designed to offer “breathing space” for people and hospitality businesses, such as the Stubshaw club, from the cost of living crisis – a move which has unsurprisingly been welcomed by the Parliamentary Labour Party.

Polling has suggested that the party is enjoying something of a ‘Burnham bounce’ as well, narrowing the gap with Reform to two points in More in Common’s latest figures.

open image in gallery Andy Burnham (right) and John Healey during a visit to the Hare pub in Harlow, Essex ( PA )

The new prime minister, who has set out his stall to “rewire Britain” and move power out of the nation’s capital to its regions as he promises the most significant political change for almost half a century, has seen his own personal approval rating rise to plus 13 - higher than Sir Keir’s ever was.

“What Andy has put his finger on is that you can't just manage a country from Westminster and Whitehall”, Mr Hurley said.

“You can't just sign a bit of paper in your office in Downing Street and suddenly the country has changed for the better. It's painstaking hard work from the grassroots up.”

The Stubshaw Cross club is the representation of those grassroots, according to Mr Hurley, and he believes Mr Burnham is far more comfortable among them – and understands them better – than his predecessor.

He said: “One of his campaign slogans in Makerfield was ‘Things will get better if we stick together’.

open image in gallery "Vote Andy For Us" Labour by-election campaign placards depicting Andy Burnham adorn the campaign HQ at Stubshaw Cross Community and Sports Club in May ( Getty )

“It pinpointed to me the difference between Andy's approach and the approach of Labour governments over the past 30 years.

“In '97, the slogan was ‘Things can only get better’. There's a sense there that things are going to get better, there is going to be this guiding hand of progress whether you like it or not, and all you need to do, the working class of the Midlands and the North, is sit back and progress will be done to you.

“Whereas Andy's vision of things getting better is very much contingent on the collective, very much contingent on saying things will get better if we stick together.”

A northern cabinet and a northern outpost

“The London set have run it for too long”, Mr Burnham said of his party in an interview with The Observer during his by-election campaign.

He has since, perhaps pointedly, appointed a cabinet stacked with MPs from Greater Manchester, Merseyside and Yorkshire.

About Mr Burnham’s overtly northern reset of the Labour Party, Liverpool City Region mayor and close friend of the prime minister Steve Rotheram told The Independent earlier this month: “There's no doubt about it - it'll wind some people up.”

But the new leader is only utilising the “broad church” on which Labour prides itself, according to his former mayoral colleague.

“It doesn't matter whether you've left school at 16 with few formal qualifications or you've been lucky enough to go to Oxbridge,” he said. “The party should attract everybody if they have the same values.

“Andy's got Labour values. He wants the best for people and he wants the country to prosper, but he wants to take people with him and tackle some of the thorny issues.”

open image in gallery Heron House, in Albert Square, which will be the interim base of the British government's 'Number 10 of the North' ( Getty )

Central to his northern revolution is Number 10 North – the prime minister’s Manchester outpost, which he has said will be the “conduit” through which he redistributes power across the UK.

“The days of Whitehall resisting devolution are over, for good”, the prime minister said before his first meeting there on Friday, as he promised it would move influence away from Westminster and Whitehall “by putting more power into every postcode across the entire country.”

Hoping to benefit from its proximity to Liverpool is Mr Rotheram.

“I think its location is totemic for Andy for what he wants to do with that Manchesterism and growing that”, the mayor said. “But its function will be more important than its geography.

open image in gallery Andy Burnham, greets Mayor of the Liverpool City Region, Steve Rotheram and his grandson ( Getty )

“That would be really helpful, if all of a sudden somewhere was recognised that you can go there and speak to government rather than always go down to SW1 and speak to government.”

The prime minister’s focus on the city he used to lead is not surprising. He also invited Donald Trump to his old stomping ground when it hosts the G20 next year - but does it mean that Manchester is well and truly now England’s second city?

West Midlands mayor Richard Parker rejects the suggestion that its rise could come at Birmingham’s expense.

“To be really clear, Andy Burnham is now the prime minister for the country, and he can only succeed if the country succeeds”, Mr Parker told The Independent.

“The best way I can do that is working with him to ensure the West Midlands succeeds, and that's my priority. I'm really positive about devolution and the impact the prime minister has made so far in his days in office.

open image in gallery The Millstone pub in central Manchester installed a replica front door of Number 10 Downing Street ( PA )

“I'm not going to get fixated on Number 10 North”, he added. “It’s there to deliver growth, investment, and prosperity for our regions, and I see that as a real positive.”

Mr Burnham’s advocacy for devolution and a commitment to a markedly different approach to his predecessor are the primary reasons for his rise to the country’s highest office, Mr Parker believes.

“Andy was pretty clear about that [a different focus from Sir Keir], and actually I think that projection, or that focus and recognition, is the reason why he's become prime minister”, he said.

‘A Labour government with a bit of urgency’

In Mr Rotheram’s eyes, Mr Burnham’s political abilities, more so than his politics, contrast with the man who returned Labour to government in 2024.

The mayor was critical of the previous administration’s communication but he believes his friend can remedy that.

“Andy can connect”, he said. “Having Andy as the leader, we'll be able therefore to use the messaging that we've previously failed to connect with, to try and ensure that we get on doorsteps and tell people how Labour can change people's lives with Andy Burnham as the prime minister.”

For Mr Hurley, the approach in the first week’s administration underlines why those within the Labour Party are daring to get their hopes up – albeit cautiously.

“It’s a Labour government with a bit of urgency, which has been sadly missing in action over the past six to 12 months”, he said.

open image in gallery Andy Burnham visits the Hare Inn with chancellor John Healey, in Harlow, Essex ( Reuters )

“My criticism of the previous prime minister, he came in with a lot of good intentions, but too often I think there wasn't the sense of urgency that was needed.”

“Keir got off to a bad start. Some decisions out of Number 11 for the first six months weren't the most optimal.

“But he also gave a speech in the Rose Garden at Downing Street in August 2024 - he'd been in for about six weeks - and said, ‘Things are going to get worse, and things aren't as good as you want them to be.’ It took the wind out of people's sails a little bit.

“Under Andy, there is a contingent sense of cautious optimism and hope here.

“It's not blind, it's not naive. It's knowing full well that this is going to be an incredibly, incredibly difficult thing that we're going to do for the country.

“But bit by bit, step by step, if we stick together, things will get better.”

Former minister Lord John Horam has died at the age of 87, his family says.

The peer died at St Mary’s Hospital in Paddington, London, after falling on the way home from a day working at the House of Lords on 2 July.

Despite receiving care from paramedics and hospital staff, he did not regain consciousness, his family said.

Lord Horam was born in Preston, Lancashire, and was head boy at the independent Silcoates School.

He went on to read economics at Cambridge, gaining an MA in 1960.

open image in gallery John Horam, pictured in 1976 when he was Labour's Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Transport ( Getty )

His first job was with the confectionery brand Rowntree’s, where he worked on developing the After Eight mint.

He then had a stint in journalism, writing for the Financial Times and The Economist, before entering politics.

Lord Horam represented three parties in Parliament. He was the Labour and later Social Democratic Party (SDP) MP for Gateshead between 1970 and 1983, before defecting to the Conservatives in 1987, serving as Tory MP for Orpington from 1992 to 2010.

He was a minister in both Labour and Conservative governments.

Lord Horam was created a working life peer as Baron Horam of Grimsargh in 2013.

In the Lords, he advocated for increased housing, a living wage, and raising the income tax threshold.

He was a member of the Conservative European Mainstream Group and was a staunch supporter of the UK remaining in the EU.

He was also a member of the Common Sense Group of Conservative Parliamentarians, which campaigns for a crackdown on immigration and opposes what it deems “woke ideology”.

In 1987, he married Judith Jackson, the former motoring editor of The Sunday Times and The Guardian.

He was stepfather to her sons Fraser and Lincoln – the latter of whom is now the Conservative MP for Spelthorne, having been elected in 2024.

“John’s widow Judith (née Jackson) and stepsons Fraser and Lincoln Jopp would like to thank the paramedics, police and all the staff at St Mary’s for the immaculate care John received,” a family statement said.

Economics has a term for what U.S. grocery prices have done in recent years: rockets and feathers.

Rockets, because the cost of food eaten at home zoomed up in the aftermath of the pandemic. Feathers, because once prices rise, they’re slow to come down.

That’s been frustrating for Americans hit with the sharpest increase in grocery prices in 50 years. While food price inflation peaked in 2022, when prices jumped 11.4%, prices have not reversed course. An acceleration in flation after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran has prolonged the aggravation.

“I think the public is coming to grips with, ‘Well, I’m hearing inflation has slowed, but things aren’t getting any cheaper.’ It has to be deflation for prices to go down, and that’s very rare,” said Matt Hamory, who leads the global grocery practice at the consulting company AlixPartners.

Prices for food at home are expected to rise 2.7% across the country this year, the U.S. Department of Agriculture reported Friday. That's higher than the grocery inflation shoppers saw in 2024 and 2025 but close to the historical average of 2.6%.

It's the compounding effect of the post-pandemic price shocks that consumers are still feeling, and they're reacting to them in ways that could have repercussions for the U.S. economy.

A recent study by the consulting firm Bain & Co. and the market research company NielsenIQ said the number of items purchased at U.S. grocery stores declined in the second half of last year and dropped more sharply starting in February of this year. The study said high gas prices, rising GLP-1 usage and cuts in the number of people receiving government food aid are all affecting grocery spending.

Consumers are also looking for deals and shopping around to find them. In the second quarter of this year, discounters like Costco, Walmart and Aldi took market share away from traditional grocers like Kroger and Albertsons, according to Numerator, a market research firm.

Many U.S. shoppers are also replacing name-brand products with store brands to save money. Total sales of store brands at supermarkets, drugstores and other retailers grew to a record $282.8 billion last year, the Private Label Manufacturers Association said.

“Now that this option becomes available, why would I go back? You have the convenience, it’s the same, but my cost is 40% less and it’s a brand that I know and trust,” said Sean Hooper, a senior solution principal at Relex Solutions, a retail and grocery consulting firm.

Prices rocketed up for lots of reasons in the wake of the pandemic, from the war in Ukraine to a highly contagious bird flu that pushed retail egg prices to record highs last year. And when prices rocket upward — whether for food, gas or other items — consumers can count on a slow, downy descent.

For one thing, retailers are reluctant to lower prices on inventory they ordered when wholesale prices were high, said Jared Bernstein, a senior policy fellow at the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy who served as chair of President Joe Biden’s Council of Economic Advisers.

Stores and food companies also want to maximize their profits and were reluctant to give up some of the sales gains they saw after the pandemic, Bernstein said. PepsiCo hiked its prices by double-digit percentages for eight straight quarters in 2022 and 2023, for example, citing higher ingredient and packaging costs. After customer demand faltered, the company began lowering prices on some snacks last year.

Customer behavior also can contribute to prices staying elevated. When prices spike, people shop around for lower ones. But consumers often stop deal hunting when they see prices coming down, giving retailers less incentive to lower prices even further.

“There’s less competitive force on the feather side of the mountain,” Bernstein said.

In some cases, grocery inflation is the result of long-term issues with no quick fix. Consider the average price of coffee, which has risen 54% in U.S. cities since 2019, according to government data. Climate issues — including drought in Vietnam, heavy rain in Indonesia and hot, dry weather in Brazil — are blamed for reducing coffee yields and driving up global prices.

In other cases, there are clearer causes and simpler fixes. For example, U.S. consumers paid 19.5% more for fresh tomatoes in June compared to a year earlier due to a 17% import tax the Trump administration placed on fresh tomatoes from Mexico. Coffee was subject to a tariff for most of 2025 as well, but the duty was eventually removed.

Hamory said the feather may be starting to fall as big retailers invest in price cuts. In early July, Walmart said it was rolling back prices on ground beef, corn, red cherries, ice cream, potato chips and Coca-Cola and Pepsi products. Target also cut prices on some foods in March.

“If the big guys are really investing, saying, ‘That’s what I need to do to get right with my customer,' that will force others in the market to act," Hamory said. “It’s just in the process of starting, but that’s a thing we could be seeing.”

News.title: Britain to pay higher Trump tariffs than EU
News.content:
Britain will pay higher tariffs than the EU after Donald Trump’s latest global trade onslaught.

Bosses in Britain have warned they will lose any competitive advantage over the bloc after the US President announced higher import taxes on goods from 60 trading partners.

The US administration imposed 10pc tariffs on both Britain and the EU to replace levies which expired overnight following a Supreme Court ruling earlier this year.

Britain must pay the import taxes on top of so-called Most Favoured Nation tariffs imposed on all members of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

However, from Friday, the EU’s tariffs are inclusive of the WTO levies. The average WTO tariff rate is between 2.4pc to 3.5pc for non-agricultural food products.

William Bain, head of trade policy at the BCC, said: “There will be concerns about the loss of the UK’s competitive advantage over the EU and other countries which have secured a more favourable deal in other goods sectors.”

A government spokesman said: “There is no negative ‌change ‌to ⁠the tariff rate facing UK businesses as a result of this ⁠announcement.”

“Our agreement with the US remains in place, and today we see ​an improvement to our ‌trading terms with zero tariffs on whisky and medical technology.”

Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, said Scottish whisky distilleries would get a “boost” from the new tariff regime, which removes levies on scotch under a deal first announced during the King’s state visit to the US in April.

On Friday, Trump also threatened new tariffs on the European Union in response to billions worth of fines imposed on US tech giants by competition regulators.

In a post on his social media platform Truth Social, Trump said: “The United States of America is not a “PIGGYBANK” for Europe, nor will we allow it to be!”

The US president said he expected to impose “substantial tariffs” on the EU after the European Commission fined Google €890m (£760m) on Thursday.

UK and European stock markets shrugged off the latest tariffs, with the FTSE 100 up 0.9pc.

However, Wall Street was more mixed. The S&P 500 was roughly flat, while the Nasdaq Composite was down 1.1pc. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 0.3pc near the end of Friday’s trading session.

It followed dramatic falls in Asia overnight, with Japan’s Nikkei falling 2.7pc and South Korea’s Kospi down 5.7pc.

News.title: Mason Mount offering Michael Carrick a midfield solution which could have legs
News.content:
It is not uncommon to hear football club executives talking about the importance of the “money being on the pitch”.

In other words, managers having their best players fit and available most if not all of the time. Quality at the top level is essential but so is robustness. They go hand in hand.

Unfortunately for Manchester United, the money has not been on the pitch down the years nearly as much as the club would want or expect.

Bruno Fernandes stands out for what he does with the ball primarily, but also because he plays almost every minute of every game and, while his sheer indefatigability is extreme, United know they need more of his ilk.

This is why the forthcoming season is such a big one for Mason Mount. His quality has seldom been in doubt. The problem is he has rarely been on the pitch long or consistently enough to show it.

Indeed, the one-time England midfielder has started just 25 Premier League matches since his £60m move from Chelsea three years ago and that perennial unavailability is one of the reasons doubts were being cast about his Old Trafford future going into this summer.

Yet Michael Carrick was keen to keep Mount, United have rebuffed inquiries around him and intriguingly the 27-year-old could yet have an impact on what the club do during the remaining six weeks of the transfer window.

For the second time in the space of six days, Mount was deployed in a deeper midfield role alongside new £48m, signing Andrey Santos for Friday’s resounding 5-0 victory over Norwegian side Rosenborg in Trondheim, just as he had done against Wrexham last weekend.

News.title: Eleanor Cardwell: ‘Comfortable sportswear should not be expensive’
News.content:
What sports shoes do you recommend?

Robert, South West

The sports shoes that I’m currently wearing are from Puma. They’re very comfortable and have support. I actually wear a basketball shoe at the minute to have more support up the ankle.

A lot of the girls wear Asics as well, which I know is the netball shoe. I’ve worn Puma for the last four years, so I would recommend them.

But honestly, whatever works best for you, you have to try them out. Whatever is best for your instep and whatever is comfiest. And if you need more ankle support, you can put some ankle braces on.

How has playing for Manchester Thunder helped you develop as a player?

Jason, London

Manchester has massively helped me develop as a player. I’ve been playing here since 2012. As a young girl, it created me as a person, to be honest with you. It’s such a family environment that I think a lot of my values come from this club. So my family values, being connected, creating energy – all those things come rooted from this club, which is incredible.

I think whatever step you are in your career, whether you’re a young athlete or senior, they help you develop. Even now I’m 31, they’re still helping me learn new things on the court. The coaches are incredible, and I’m constantly learning and being inspired by them every single week.

Do players retire from elite netball quite young?

Helen, South West

I think it depends on the athlete. Some can retire at 40, and that’s because their bodies are so conditioned, and they might not have had any major injuries in their career. They’re able to continue to push themselves all the way until 40.

But I’d say the average is probably mid-30s. Now the Super League has become professional, the younger athletes are getting better training from a younger age. We want to keep pushing ourselves to play as long as possible.

How can netball get more coverage when women’s football is constantly pushed?

Sarah, South West

I think netball needs to have more sponsors to get more media coverage. Bigger sponsors.

Players need to put their personalities more out there on social media, so brands will want to work with us. Everyone’s got amazing personalities in netball. They [brands] should want to be a part of the netball players’ stories and the netball teams.

But it’s about getting as much exposure as possible, and making sure that everyone is going on YouTube or BBC, so more people are able to learn about the sport.

I loved netball at school. How do I get involved now in my 60s?

Sue, Yorkshire

Netball is for everyone. I personally love going to walking netball sessions and taking them through classes. You can go to the England Netball website and find out where you can play locally.

There’s also Back to Netball, depending on your ability and what you want to get out of it. Personally, I think walking netball is so much fun. The women who are in those sessions are a huge laugh, and I know when I retire, I’m going to be joining a group, for sure.

Apart from netball, what other hobbies do you have? How do they help you relieve the pressure of competition?

George, London

I feel like over the past few years I’ve really got into some new hobbies. I love reading. I love fantasy reading, like Throne of Glass. I love BookTok, so I’ve really got into that.

I’m also very crafty. I like making things – I’ve made little crochet bees for all the girls, and I like drawing, and painting occasionally – just wholesome activities to take me away from netball life. As soon as I zone in on an activity, I’m locked in and I have to complete it.
