Vports Espirito Santo: A Record First Half

Vports is the private operator that manages the port complex in Brazil’s southeastern state of Espirito Santo. The company took over the concession in a landmark privatization, becoming the country’s only fully private port authority.

For foreign investors and expats unfamiliar with the region, the complex is not a single dock but a network of terminals. It spans the cities of Vitoria, the state capital, and neighboring Vila Velha, along with the Port of Barra do Riacho and the Praia Mole terminal.

This multi-site footprint allows Vports to handle a diverse cargo mix. The complex serves as a strategic gateway for Brazil’s industrial heartland, connecting mining, agriculture, and manufacturing to global markets.

Breaking Down The Record Cargo Mix

The 4.1 million tonnes moved in the first half of 2026 reflects a sharp pivot toward higher-value industrial and energy-related cargo. Vports reported that offshore-linked cargo surged 202% in the first quarter, driven by what the company called “the heating up of the oil and gas industry.”

Concentrated mineral cargoes jumped 108% year-on-year in the same period. Pig iron exports rose 94%, while granite block shipments increased 60%. These figures underscore Espirito Santo’s role as a key outlet for Brazil’s mineral wealth.

Vehicle handling doubled, with imports and exports flowing through Vitoria and Vila Velha. Fertilizer imports climbed 45%, machinery rose 83%, and general equipment shipments grew 39%.

January 2026 data provided an early signal of the trend. The Vitoria and Vila Velha terminals alone moved 700,000 tonnes that month, up 15% year-on-year. Solid bulk cargo accounted for 352,000 tonnes, a 28% increase.

Offshore Oil And Gas Fuels The Surge

The standout performer in the first half was offshore support logistics. Vports directly attributed the 202% spike in offshore cargo to increased activity in Brazil’s oil and gas sector.

Espirito Santo sits near key offshore basins, making the complex a natural hub for supplying rigs, transporting equipment, and moving materials for exploration and production. The rebound in global energy investment has channeled more traffic through Vitoria and Vila Velha.

This segment requires specialized handling and storage, capabilities Vports has been expanding. The growth signals that international energy firms are routing more supply-chain activity through the state.

Investment Plan: R$500 Million To Expand Capacity

Vports has committed to investing more than R$500 million (~US$98 million) by 2027. The goal is to boost cargo-handling capacity by 80% over a five-year period.

The capital expenditure plan covers terminal upgrades, new equipment, and improved rail connectivity. Brazilian port press has separately reported R$180 million (~US$35.3 million) in port works underway in Espirito Santo, reinforcing the broader infrastructure push.

Rail links are a critical piece of the strategy. Better rail connections would allow minerals, agricultural goods, and industrial products to reach the docks more efficiently from inland states such as Minas Gerais.

Vports’ long-term target, according to company statements cited in local media, is to achieve major throughput growth at the Port of Vitoria by 2029. The 2026 half-year record suggests the operator is on track.

Outpacing National Averages

The Espirito Santo complex has consistently grown faster than Brazil’s port sector as a whole. In 2024, Vports moved 8.4 million tonnes, a 15% increase compared to a national average of just 2%.

That year already set records for imports, solid bulk, and vehicle handling. The 2026 first-half performance builds on that momentum, with a more diversified cargo base insulating the complex from downturns in any single commodity.

Industrial imports, agricultural and mining-linked cargo, offshore support, and a rising vehicle business together make Espirito Santo one of Brazil’s most dynamic logistics corridors. For international traders and investors, the complex offers a fast-growing alternative to the country’s more congested southern ports.

What The Record Means For Foreign Investors

The throughput record is a tangible signal that privatization is delivering results. Vports’ ability to attract diverse cargo types – from granite blocks to complex oilfield equipment – demonstrates operational flexibility that state-run ports often struggle to match.

For expats and foreign businesses looking at Brazilian logistics, the Espirito Santo complex offers a case study in how private management can unlock capacity. The 80% expansion target and rail investments point to further growth ahead.

The offshore surge also highlights Brazil’s enduring appeal as an energy investment destination. As global oil majors maintain or increase spending on Brazilian basins, demand for specialized port services in Espirito Santo is likely to remain strong.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Vports?

Vports is the private operator of the port complex in Espirito Santo, Brazil. It is the country’s only fully private port authority, managing terminals in Vitoria, Vila Velha, Barra do Riacho, and Praia Mole.

How much cargo did Vports handle in the first half of 2026?

Vports handled approximately 4.1 million tonnes in the first half of 2026, a record for the period and a 12% increase compared to the same timeframe in 2025.

What is driving growth at the Espirito Santo port complex?

Growth is driven by a diversified cargo mix including offshore oil and gas logistics, concentrated minerals, pig iron, granite blocks, vehicles, fertilizers, and machinery. The offshore segment alone rose 202% in Q1 2026.

World.title: Cerro Verde First-Half Net Income Hits US$501.5 Million
World.content:
Peru · Companies

Key Facts —Net Income US$501.5 million for the first half of 2026. —Copper Production 202.9 million pounds in the first half. —Realized Copper Price US$6.55 per pound. —Capital Expenditures US$168.3 million in property, plant and equipment. —Freeport-McMoRan Control Combined stake of 55.66% after a Q2 share purchase.

Cerro Verde first half results for 2026 show Sociedad Minera Cerro Verde, the giant Peruvian copper mine controlled by U.S.-based Freeport-McMoRan, generated a net income of US$501.5 million. The strong earnings, reported in late July, were fueled by a favorable realized copper price of US$6.55 per pound, which offset a slight decline in production volumes.

An open-pit copper mine in Peru (illustrative); Cerro Verde is one of the country’s largest copper producers. Photo: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA.

Cerro Verde First-Half Results

Sociedad Minera Cerro Verde operates one of Peru’s largest copper mines, located in the southern region of Arequipa. For international investors and expats unfamiliar with the asset, it is a cornerstone of the country’s mining sector and a major global copper producer.

The open-pit mine extracts and processes copper ore into concentrates and cathodes. Its strategic importance is underscored by its ownership: a majority stake is held by Freeport-McMoRan, the U.S. mining heavyweight, through its subsidiaries Freeport Mineral and Cyprus Climax, which together control 55.66%.

Other key shareholders include SMM Cerro Verde Netherlands B.V., an affiliate of Sumitomo Metal Mining, with a 21% stake, and Compañía de Minas Buenaventura, a major Peruvian precious metals producer, holding 19%. This structure makes Cerro Verde a critical link between global mining capital and Peru’s local economy.

Production and Sales Volumes

Copper production for the first half of 2026 reached 202.9 million pounds. This figure represents a slight decrease compared to previous periods, a detail noted in Peruvian financial press reports.

Copper sales volume totaled 195.4 million pounds for the half-year. The gap between production and sales is a normal operational variance, reflecting the timing of concentrate shipments from the Arequipa site to global customers.

Beyond copper, the mine also produces molybdenum as a significant by-product. The realized molybdenum price for the period was US$31.5 per pound, providing an additional, though smaller, revenue stream alongside the primary copper output.

Revenue Driver: Copper Price Realization

The standout figure driving the US$501.5 million net income was the realized copper price. Cerro Verde sold its copper at an average of US$6.55 per pound during the first six months of 2026.

This price level reflects a strong global copper market, where demand for the red metal – essential for electrification and construction – has kept prices elevated. The company’s ability to realize a price close to global benchmarks is crucial for its profitability.

While a precise total net sales revenue figure was not directly quoted in the available filings, the combination of 195.4 million pounds sold and a US$6.55/lb price indicates robust revenue generation. This top-line strength was the primary engine behind the half-year earnings.

Cost Management and Capital Spending

The company deployed US$168.3 million in capital expenditures for property, plant, and equipment during the half. This investment level signals ongoing commitment to sustaining and potentially expanding the mine’s long-term production capacity.

A directly quoted unit cash cost for the first half was not available in the initial reporting. However, the strong net income margin suggests that operating costs were well-managed against the backdrop of a high realized copper price.

Cost control remains a central focus for mining operations in Peru, where inflation and logistical expenses can pressure margins. Cerro Verde’s ability to convert a high copper price into substantial net income points to effective operational management.

Ownership Structure and Strategic Moves

The ownership structure saw a minor adjustment during the second quarter. Cyprus Climax, a Freeport-McMoRan subsidiary, purchased 2 million shares, lifting the combined Freeport-side stake from 55.08% to 55.66%.

This incremental purchase reinforces Freeport’s control over the asset. For foreign portfolio investors, this signals the parent company’s continued confidence in Cerro Verde’s long-term value and cash flow generation potential.

The other major shareholders maintained their positions. SMM Cerro Verde Netherlands B.V. holds 21%, and Buenaventura retains its 19% stake. This stable shareholder base supports the mine’s strategic direction and governance.

Outlook and Regional Impact

The first-half performance positions Cerro Verde for a potentially strong full-year 2026, contingent on copper prices holding steady. The mine’s output is a primary driver of Peru’s mining GDP and a key source of tax revenue for the Arequipa region.

A January 2026 board dividend of US$500 million, based on accumulated results through September 2025, was reported in the press. While a first-half 2026 dividend was not confirmed, the mine’s history of large distributions is a critical factor for investors evaluating its income potential.

For expats and international observers in Peru, Cerro Verde’s financial health directly impacts local development. The mining canon, a tax redistribution mechanism, funds infrastructure and social projects in Arequipa, making the mine’s profitability a matter of broad regional importance.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was Cerro Verde’s net income in the first half of 2026?

Sociedad Minera Cerro Verde reported a net income of US$501.5 million for the first half of 2026, driven by strong copper prices.

Who owns the Cerro Verde copper mine in Peru?

The mine is controlled by U.S.-based Freeport-McMoRan through subsidiaries Freeport Mineral and Cyprus Climax, which hold a combined 55.66% stake. Sumitomo Metal Mining’s SMM Cerro Verde Netherlands B.V. holds 21%, and Peru’s Buenaventura holds 19%.

How much copper did Cerro Verde produce in the first half of 2026?

The mine produced 202.9 million pounds of copper and achieved a sales volume of 195.4 million pounds. The realized copper price averaged US$6.55 per pound.

World.title: Jamaica BPO Sector Loses US$220 Million, 5,000 Jobs
World.content:
Jamaica · Business

Key Facts —Spending Drop Local spending in the Jamaica BPO sector fell by roughly US$220 million to about US$780 million in the fiscal year ended March 2026. —Job Losses Employment dropped to approximately 50,000 from 62,000 two years earlier, with some industry counts suggesting a fall to 40,000. —Company Closures The number of operating firms declined from more than 90 to about 70 by March 2026. —Economic Weight The sector is Jamaica’s second-largest employer and third-largest source of foreign exchange, historically generating about US$1 billion annually. —Government Response A multi-agency task force was created to address job losses and help workers adapt to artificial intelligence.

The Jamaica BPO sector, long a pillar of the island’s foreign-exchange earnings, has suffered a sharp contraction, losing roughly US$220 million in local spending and about 5,000 jobs in the fiscal year that ended in March 2026.

Kingston, Jamaica from above; the island’s business-process outsourcing sector is contracting. Photo: Wikimedia Commons (public domain).

Inside the Jamaica BPO Contraction

For foreign investors and expats, Jamaica’s global digital services sector – widely known as business-process outsourcing or BPO – has been one of the country’s most reliable economic engines. The industry operates large call centres and back-office hubs, primarily serving North American clients from special economic zones in Kingston, Montego Bay, and Portmore.

Before the recent downturn, the sector employed roughly 60,000 people and generated about US$1 billion in foreign exchange annually. Government estimates showed that roughly 80% of that revenue, or US$720 million, stayed in the local economy, with about 70% of the total going directly to wages.

This made BPO Jamaica’s second-largest employer and its third-largest source of foreign currency, trailing only tourism and remittances. The industry’s rapid growth over the past decade transformed it from a niche service provider into a cornerstone of formal employment for young, English-speaking Jamaicans.

The Scale of the Contraction

Data from the government’s annual Form 18-K filing, reported by The Jamaica Observer on July 24, 2026, paints a sobering picture. Local spending by the sector fell to approximately US$780 million in the fiscal year ending March 2026, down from roughly US$1 billion a year earlier.

Employment also slid. The official count showed about 50,000 workers remaining, down from 62,000 two years prior. The number of active companies shrank from more than 90 to roughly 70 over the same period.

A separate industry census cited by Yoni Epstein, president of the Global Services Association of Jamaica (GSAJ), suggested an even steeper decline. Speaking to the Jamaica Gleaner in mid-July, Epstein said the workforce had dropped to about 40,000, down from 60,000 a few years back. The discrepancy likely reflects different counting methodologies between government and industry bodies.

What Is Driving the Decline

The government’s filing attributes the losses to a mix of onshoring and reshoring by US clients, geopolitical considerations, technological advancements, the impact of Hurricane Melissa, and local cost-of-doing-business challenges. The hurricane, which disrupted operations, compounded existing structural pressures.

Crucially, GSAJ’s Epstein pushed back on the narrative that artificial intelligence is the primary culprit. He told the Financial Gleaner that low productivity, the hurricane’s aftermath, and a tight labour market with limited available talent were the main drivers. “AI was not the main cause” of the job losses, he stated.

Still, the government is not ignoring automation. In early July, Minister Pernell Charles Jr. announced a new task force to address job losses and the growing impact of AI. He argued that workers must become more compatible with AI tools so the technology boosts productivity rather than simply displacing jobs.

The broader trend of nearshoring shifts is partly reflected in the official reference to onshoring and reshoring. As US companies face political pressure to bring service jobs back home or move them closer to American soil, Jamaica faces stiffer competition from destinations in Latin America and the Caribbean.

The Industry and Government Response

The GSAJ has outlined a three-point recovery plan. First, it aims to restore investor confidence through targeted marketing that reinforces Jamaica’s value proposition. Second, it will push to upskill the workforce, moving agents from routine call handling toward more complex knowledge-process outsourcing (KPO) tasks. Third, it wants to reduce operating expenses to improve the country’s cost competitiveness.

The government is moving in parallel. A working group now includes representatives from the GDS sector, the Port Authority of Jamaica (PAJ), the investment promotion agency JAMPRO, and the Jamaica Special Economic Zone Authority (JSEZA). Its mandate has expanded from three focus areas to six, with a central goal of shifting the job mix toward higher-value work.

Officials want to change the sector’s composition from an 80:20 ratio of basic BPO to KPO work toward a 60:40 split. This implies a significant reskilling effort, moving employees into areas like accounting, legal process support, and data analytics. The July 7 government response emphasized helping workers adapt to AI rather than treating automation only as a threat.

What This Means for Foreign Investors and Expats

For foreigners with business interests in Jamaica, the BPO contraction signals a period of adjustment rather than collapse. The sector still employs tens of thousands and generates hundreds of millions in foreign exchange. However, the loss of 5,000 to 20,000 jobs – depending on which count one uses – will ripple through consumer spending and real estate in BPO-heavy areas like Montego Bay and Portmore.

Investors in Jamaican special economic zones should watch the government’s push toward KPO closely. The shift to higher-value services could create demand for more skilled, better-paid workers, potentially tightening the labour market for educated professionals. It may also open niches for training providers and technology vendors.

The US$220 million drop in local spending is significant for an economy where BPO contributed roughly 6% of GDP, or about J$136 billion (~US$870 million). Yet the sector’s fundamentals – English fluency, proximity to US time zones, and established infrastructure – remain intact. The question is whether Jamaica can adapt quickly enough to a global market that is rewiring itself around AI and political demands for domestic job creation.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many jobs has the Jamaica BPO sector lost?

Official government data shows employment fell to about 50,000 in March 2026, down from 62,000 two years earlier – a loss of roughly 12,000 positions. The industry association GSAJ cites a steeper decline to about 40,000 jobs from a peak of 60,000.

Is artificial intelligence the main cause of job losses in Jamaica’s call centres?

No, according to GSAJ president Yoni Epstein. He stated that AI was not the main cause. He pointed instead to low productivity, Hurricane Melissa, a tight labour market, and reshoring by US clients as the primary drivers.

How is the Jamaican government responding to the BPO contraction?

The government created a multi-agency task force including JAMPRO, the Port Authority, and the special economic zone authority. Its mandate covers six areas, including shifting the workforce from basic BPO to higher-value knowledge process outsourcing (KPO) and helping workers adapt to AI tools.

Sources & Further Reading

Jamaica Gleaner · Jamaica Observer

World.title: Colombia’s Ecopetrol Board Adds Velasquez in Governance Reset
World.content:
Colombia · Companies

Key Facts —Appointee Jorge Mario Velásquez Jaramillo, former president of Colombian cement and infrastructure group Grupo Argos, was named to the Ecopetrol board on 24 July 2026. —Political context The appointment is the first board pick by president-elect Abelardo de la Espriella, who takes office in August 2026, signaling a governance reset at the 88.5% state-owned oil company. —Board departures Directors Ángela María Robledo Gómez and Tatiana Roa Avendaño, both seen as aligned with outgoing President Gustavo Petro, resigned effective 31 July 2026. —CEO exit Ricardo Roa Barragán left the presidency and CEO role on 30 July 2026, with Juan Carlos Hurtado Parra named acting president the following day. —New chair Luis Felipe Henao Cardona, described as close to the president-elect, assumed the board chairmanship on 1 August 2026.

Ecopetrol board member Jorge Mario Velásquez Jaramillo, the former president of Colombian industrial conglomerate Grupo Argos, was announced on 24 July 2026 as the first board appointment by president-elect Abelardo de la Espriella, part of a sweeping leadership overhaul at Colombia’s state-controlled oil company just days before the new government takes power.

Inside the Ecopetrol Board Change

Jorge Mario Velásquez Jaramillo is an industrial engineer from the Escuela de Ingeniería de Antioquia, now Universidad EIA, with a specialization focused on the cement industry in England.

He holds executive education credentials from the Kellogg School of Management, Stanford University, and the Universidad de los Andes senior government program.

Velásquez led Grupo Argos, a major Colombian cement, energy, and infrastructure group, from 2016 to 2026, capping more than 30 years at the company.

His board experience includes directorships at Colombian energy company Celsia, road-concession operator Odinsa, insurance and financial services firm Suramericana, and the Proantioquia foundation.

President-elect De la Espriella presented Velásquez in Medellín as a representative of the incoming government’s approach to managing the state oil company.

A Board in Flux

Ecopetrol’s board is formally a nine-member body appointed by the general shareholders’ meeting, with the Colombian state holding an 88.5% stake.

The late-July reshuffle removes two directors closely associated with outgoing President Gustavo Petro’s agenda: Ángela María Robledo Gómez and Tatiana Roa Avendaño, both of whom resigned effective 31 July 2026.

Their exits follow the departure of Ricardo Roa Barragán, who left the presidency and CEO role on 30 July 2026 after a tenure shadowed by investigations into alleged campaign-finance and influence-peddling issues tied to the previous administration.

Luis Felipe Henao Cardona, described in Colombian media as close to the president-elect, took over as board chairman on 1 August 2026.

Juan Carlos Hurtado Parra was named acting president from 31 July 2026, giving the incoming government a clean slate at the top of the company.

The board had already been in flux earlier in 2026: an extraordinary shareholders’ meeting in February elected Ángela Robledo as chairwoman and Hildebrando Vélez Galeano as vice chairman, underscoring how rapidly the governance landscape has shifted.

Political and Governance Context

Ecopetrol is Colombia’s largest company and a critical source of government revenue, making its board composition a deeply political matter with each change of administration.

The outgoing Petro government had pushed for an energy transition agenda that at times put it at odds with the oil-and-gas sector, while the incoming De la Espriella administration is expected to take a more industry-friendly stance.

The appointment of Velásquez, a veteran of Colombia’s private-sector establishment, signals a shift in tone from the state’s main vehicle for hydrocarbon production.

For foreign investors and expats monitoring Colombian assets, Ecopetrol board changes are a key governance indicator because the company trades on both the Bogotá stock exchange and the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker EC.

The Rio Times reported earlier on the broader Ecopetrol board shakeup, including CEO Roa’s exit and the resignation of Petro-aligned directors, in a piece that detailed the accelerating leadership transition.

What the Reshuffle Means for Investors

The simultaneous departure of the CEO and two board members aligned with the previous government concentrates appointment power in the hands of the incoming administration.

Velásquez’s background at Grupo Argos, a company with deep experience in infrastructure and energy through its subsidiaries Celsia and Odinsa, suggests a board focus on operational and financial discipline.

Colombian media framed the appointment as part of a broader governance reset, though market reaction was not immediately quantifiable in the available reports.

Ecopetrol’s American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) are widely held by international institutional investors, who typically view board stability and political independence as key risk factors for state-owned enterprises in Latin America.

The new board will face immediate questions about the company’s exploration strategy, dividend policy, and its role in Colombia’s energy transition, all of which have direct implications for minority shareholders.

Looking Ahead

President-elect De la Espriella takes office in August 2026, and further board appointments are expected as the new government consolidates control over the nine-member body.

The general shareholders’ meeting retains the formal power to elect directors, but in practice the majority state shareholding means the government’s picks are almost certain to be ratified.

Foreign investors will watch closely whether the new board maintains Ecopetrol’s dividend framework and its investment-grade credit ratings, both of which have been points of tension during past political transitions.

The company has not yet announced a permanent replacement for the CEO position, leaving acting president Hurtado Parra in place while the new board settles in.

For now, the Velásquez appointment marks the first concrete signal of how the De la Espriella government intends to govern Latin America’s fourth-largest oil company by production.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was appointed to the Ecopetrol board in July 2026?

Jorge Mario Velásquez Jaramillo, the former president of Colombian cement and infrastructure group Grupo Argos, was named to the Ecopetrol board on 24 July 2026 as the first board pick by president-elect Abelardo de la Espriella.

Why did Ecopetrol board members resign in July 2026?

Directors Ángela María Robledo Gómez and Tatiana Roa Avendaño, both seen as aligned with outgoing President Gustavo Petro’s energy-transition agenda, resigned effective 31 July 2026 as part of a broader governance reset ahead of the new government taking office.

Who is Ecopetrol’s new CEO after Ricardo Roa left?

Juan Carlos Hurtado Parra was named acting president of Ecopetrol from 31 July 2026, following the departure of Ricardo Roa Barragán on 30 July 2026. A permanent CEO had not been announced at the time of the reshuffle.

World.title: Guyana Local Content: TotalTec-aHa JV Targets Exxon Oil Deals
World.content:
Guyana · Companies

Key Facts —Joint Venture Partners TotalTec Oilfield Services (technical partner) and aHa (local Guyanese partner). —Core Activities Oilfield services, workforce training, equipment supply, inspection, calibration, and shore-base logistics support. —Local Content Law Guyana’s Local Content Act mandates minimum Guyanese participation levels across 40 service categories in the petroleum sector. —Market Context The JV targets contracts in the ExxonMobil-operated Stabroek Block, where production exceeds 600,000 barrels per day. —Strategic Goal To build Guyanese ownership and technical capability in the oil-and-gas supply chain.

A new joint venture in Guyana’s rapidly expanding oil sector is set to deepen Guyana local content by combining international technical expertise with domestic ownership. TotalTec Oilfield Services, a company with a track record in the Stabroek Block, has partnered with local firm aHa to deliver oilfield services, workforce training, and logistics support, responding directly to government mandates designed to secure greater economic benefits for Guyanese citizens from the ExxonMobil-led oil boom.

An offshore oil drilling rig (illustrative); Guyana’s Exxon-led oil boom is driving demand for local content. Photo: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Inside the Guyana Local Content Joint Venture

The partnership pairs TotalTec Oilfield Services, an established technical and commercial advisory player in Guyana, with aHa, a local Guyanese entity. The model is explicitly designed to place ownership and operational control in local hands while leveraging international oilfield knowledge.

The venture’s service portfolio is built around practical, high-demand oilfield support. This includes the supply of critical equipment such as wire rope slings, valves, lifting gear, lubricants, and anti-slip products. It also provides essential technical services like the inspection of lifting equipment and the calibration of pressure gauges and relief valves.

Beyond equipment, the joint venture focuses on capacity building through targeted workforce training programs. This addresses a critical bottleneck in the sector: the shortage of skilled Guyanese labor certified for specialized oil and gas operations. By consolidating a journey that began for some partners as early as 2016, the JV aims to create a one-stop shop for operators.

Guyana’s Local Content Law Explained

For foreign investors and expatriates, understanding Guyana’s Local Content Act is essential to navigating the business landscape. Passed by the National Assembly in late 2021, the legislation mandates that oil companies and their subcontractors must meet minimum targets for using Guyanese goods, services, and labor across 40 distinct categories.

The law’s first schedule sets specific percentage requirements for Guyanese participation. These range from 90% local content for ground transportation and accommodation services to lower thresholds for highly specialized engineering and technical services. Companies must submit detailed local content plans to the government for approval.

The legislation creates a protected space for joint ventures exactly like the TotalTec-aHa partnership. By requiring international firms to team up with local companies to win contracts, the law aims to prevent the ‘resource curse’ and ensure that oil wealth translates into broad-based economic development, rather than flowing entirely to multinational corporations.

The ExxonMobil-Led Oil Boom Context

Guyana has emerged as one of the world’s fastest-growing economies, driven exclusively by offshore oil discoveries. The Stabroek Block, operated by U.S. supermajor ExxonMobil, has seen a string of world-class finds totaling over 11 billion barrels of recoverable oil equivalent.

Production began with the Liza Phase 1 development and has since expanded with Liza Phase 2 and Payara. Current output exceeds 600,000 barrels per day, with a target to surpass 1.2 million barrels per day by 2027 as new floating production, storage, and offloading (FPSO) vessels come online.

This breakneck expansion has created an insatiable demand for shore-base facilities, logistics, and supplier support. TotalTec-linked ventures have historically been positioned to capture this demand, having previously won ExxonMobil’s tender for shore base and logistics support during the Liza Phase 1 buildout. The new aHa partnership seeks to replicate and expand this success in subsequent development phases.

Strategic Importance for Foreign Investors

For the expatriate and foreign investor community, the TotalTec-aHa joint venture signals the maturation of Guyana’s oil services market. It demonstrates a viable, legally compliant blueprint for market entry: pairing foreign technical expertise with local ownership to meet statutory requirements.

The venture’s focus on training also addresses a key operational risk for international companies – the lack of a skilled local workforce. By creating a pipeline of certified Guyanese technicians, the JV reduces the long-term reliance on expensive expatriate labor, potentially lowering operating costs for all players in the basin.

Investors should view this partnership as a bellwether. As the Local Content Act is enforced more rigorously, similar structures will likely become mandatory across the supply chain, from catering and waste management to advanced subsea engineering. Early movers who establish credible local partnerships may secure a lasting competitive advantage.

Challenges and Unverified Details

Specific financial details of the joint venture, including the exact investment value and projected job creation numbers, were not publicly confirmed in the available documentation as of late July 2026. The precise announcement date also remains unverified from the supplied research material.

Despite these gaps, the strategic direction is unambiguous. The venture consolidates a business journey that began in 2016, aligning with the government’s stated goal of ensuring Guyanese benefit from ‘Guyanese oil.’ The partnership structure mirrors earlier models where TotalTec acted as the technical and commercial advisory backbone while local shareholders maintained ownership presence.

The primary challenge for the JV will be scaling operations quickly enough to meet the demands of ExxonMobil’s aggressive development timeline while maintaining international safety and quality standards. Competition from other local-international consortia is also intensifying as the scale of the Stabroek opportunity becomes globally recognized.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the purpose of Guyana’s Local Content Act?

The Local Content Act requires oil companies to use Guyanese goods, services, and labor for a minimum percentage of their operations. It covers 40 categories and aims to ensure that the economic benefits of oil production are retained within Guyana, fostering local business growth and job creation.

Who are TotalTec and aHa in the Guyana oil sector?

TotalTec Oilfield Services is an international technical advisory and services firm that has been active in Guyana since the early stages of the oil boom, notably winning logistics contracts for ExxonMobil’s Liza Phase 1. aHa is a local Guyanese partner, bringing domestic ownership and market access to the joint venture.

How does the TotalTec-aHa joint venture create jobs?

The JV creates direct employment by providing oilfield services and logistics support. Crucially, it also focuses on workforce training and capacity building, equipping Guyanese citizens with the certified technical skills needed to work in the offshore oil and gas industry, thereby expanding the local talent pool.

World.title: Peru Named Top 2026 Travel Spot by Lonely Planet
World.content:
Peru · Travel

Key Facts —Ranking Lonely Planet named Peru the #1 destination overall among the 25 best places to travel in 2026, published on October 21, 2025. —Heritage The guide specifically cited Machu Picchu and the Sacred Valley as marquee heritage draws for international visitors. —Nature Peru’s section of the Amazon rainforest was highlighted as a key part of the country’s natural appeal. —Gastronomy Lima’s globally recognized food scene was listed as a major reason to visit, reflecting Peru’s culinary reputation. —Access Improved flight routes and travel momentum were mentioned alongside Peru’s ongoing tourism recovery.

Peru top travel destination for 2026 – that is the verdict from Lonely Planet, which placed the Andean nation at the very top of its annual Best in Travel list. The ranking, published in October 2025, names Peru the #1 destination among 25 must-visit places worldwide, ahead of all other countries and regions.

Machu Picchu, Peru; Lonely Planet named the country a top travel destination for 2026. Photo: Martin St-Amant / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

Why Peru Is a Top Travel Destination for 2026

Lonely Planet’s Best in Travel list is one of the travel industry’s most closely watched annual guides. It is curated by the publisher’s global team of editors and writers, who select destinations based on compelling reasons to visit, cultural richness, and improved accessibility.

For 2026, Peru was not placed in a sub-category or niche list. It is the top-ranked destination overall in the main “25 best places to travel” selection. That means Lonely Planet sees Peru as the single most compelling country for travelers to prioritize next year.

The guide does not rely on a single headline attraction. Instead, it points to a mix of iconic heritage sites, vast natural landscapes, and a food culture that has become a global benchmark. For foreign residents and investors already in Latin America, the ranking confirms that Peru’s tourism product has matured well beyond the classic backpacker trail.

Machu Picchu and the Sacred Valley

No discussion of Peruvian tourism can start anywhere else. The 15th-century Inca citadel of Machu Picchu, perched high in the Andes, remains the country’s most recognizable symbol. Lonely Planet explicitly names it as a marquee heritage draw.

The Sacred Valley, which stretches between Cusco and Machu Picchu, is cited alongside the citadel. This corridor of Inca ruins, traditional weaving villages, and high-altitude farmland offers a deeper cultural immersion than a single-day visit to the ruins.

For expats based in Lima or foreign investors scouting opportunities, the Sacred Valley has also become a hub for boutique hotels and wellness retreats. The ranking reinforces the region’s status as a globally competitive heritage destination, not just a stopover.

The Amazon and Natural Appeal

Peru is one of the few countries where a traveler can move from Andean peaks to lowland rainforest in a single day. Lonely Planet highlights the Peruvian Amazon as a core part of the country’s natural appeal.

The Amazon basin covers roughly 60% of Peru’s territory. Gateways such as Iquitos and Puerto Maldonado offer lodge-based wildlife viewing, river cruises, and community-led ecotourism. This is not a marginal add-on to a highland itinerary; it is a primary reason to visit.

The guide’s emphasis on nature signals that Peru’s tourism recovery is not solely dependent on archaeological sites. The country’s biodiversity – from the cloud forests of Manu National Park to the Pacaya-Samiria National Reserve – is being positioned as a standalone draw for high-value travelers.

Cusco as a Cultural Gateway

Cusco, the former Inca capital, is identified by Lonely Planet as a key base for visitors and a major cultural gateway. The city sits at 3,400 meters (11,150 feet) above sea level and blends Inca stonework with Spanish colonial architecture.

Most international arrivals to the southern Andes pass through Cusco’s Alejandro Velasco Astete International Airport. The city has steadily upgraded its hotel stock, from restored convents to design-forward boutique properties. Restaurants in the historic center now rival those in Lima for ambition.

For foreign residents in Latin America, Cusco is increasingly accessible via direct flights from Lima and regional hubs. The Lonely Planet nod is likely to accelerate investment in hospitality and services, particularly as the city prepares for higher visitor volumes in 2026.

Lima’s Gastronomy as a Global Draw

Lima’s food scene is no longer a secret. Lonely Planet lists the capital’s gastronomy as a major reason to visit Peru, reflecting a reputation built over two decades by chefs such as Gastón Acurio, Virgilio Martínez, and Pía León.

The city is home to multiple restaurants ranked among the world’s best, including Central, which has topped the World’s 50 Best Restaurants list. But the culinary appeal extends far beyond fine dining. Neighborhood markets, cevicherías, and Nikkei (Japanese-Peruvian) counters offer exceptional food at every price point.

For expats already living in Lima, the ranking validates what they experience daily. For potential visitors, it reframes Peru as a food-first destination where a meal can justify the trip. The guide’s mention of gastronomy alongside Machu Picchu signals that cuisine is now a pillar of Peru’s tourism identity, not a footnote.

Tourism Recovery and Improved Access

Lonely Planet’s selection arrives as Peru’s tourism sector continues to rebuild following years of disruption from political unrest and the COVID-19 pandemic. The guide mentions new routes, improved access, and travel momentum as part of the context for Peru’s inclusion.

While exact inbound-arrival figures for 2026 are not yet available from PromPerú or Mincetur, the broader trend points to a steady recovery. Airlines have been restoring and adding frequencies to Lima’s Jorge Chávez International Airport, and regional carriers are expanding connections to Cusco and Arequipa.

The ranking itself functions as a powerful recovery signal. Travel operators, hotel groups, and foreign investors often use Lonely Planet’s list as a demand indicator. A #1 placement can translate into forward bookings, media coverage, and renewed confidence in Peru’s tourism infrastructure.

For foreigners considering a visit or investment, the message is clear: Peru is not merely open for business – it is being actively recommended by the world’s most influential travel guide as the single best place to go in 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Lonely Planet rank Peru as the top country for 2026?

Yes. Lonely Planet’s Best in Travel 2026 list named Peru the #1 destination overall among the 25 best places to travel, not just in a country-specific category.

What specific attractions did Lonely Planet highlight in Peru?

The guide cited Machu Picchu and the Sacred Valley, the Amazon rainforest, Cusco as a cultural gateway, and Lima’s gastronomy as key reasons to visit.

When was the Lonely Planet Best in Travel 2026 list published?

The list was published on October 21, 2025, as part of Lonely Planet’s annual guide for the following year.

World.title: US Lifts Mexico Cattle Ban After Screwworm Crisis
World.content:
Mexico · Trade

Key Facts —First reopening Douglas, Arizona port resumes Mexico cattle imports on August 24, 2026 —Next ports Santa Teresa and Columbus, New Mexico will reopen at unspecified later dates —Suspension trigger USDA halted imports in May 2025 after New World screwworm spread northward from Mexico —Eradication effort Mexico releases over 100 million sterile flies weekly to contain the parasite —Market impact Analysts expect only limited, short-term psychological softening of feeder cattle prices

Mexico cattle imports will resume on August 24, 2026, when the United States reopens its Douglas, Arizona port of entry to live animals, ending a 15-month suspension that disrupted North American beef supply chains and strained ranchers on both sides of the border.

Beef cattle in a pasture; the US will resume Mexican cattle imports on August 24. Photo: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

The Mexico Cattle Imports Reopening

The U.S. Department of Agriculture confirmed it will restart live cattle imports from Mexico in stages, with the Douglas, Arizona crossing opening first on August 24. Two additional ports – Santa Teresa and Columbus, both in New Mexico – will follow at later, unspecified dates.

USDA officials described the approach as a step-by-step review process. The department will reassess the screwworm situation between each reopening phase, basing decisions on case numbers and the geographic spread of the parasite.

An earlier USDA proposal had also tied the eventual reopening of crossings at Del Rio and Laredo, Texas, to additional control measures by Mexican state authorities. Those Texas ports remain closed under the current plan, with no timeline announced for their return to service.

The Screwworm Outbreak That Shut the Border

The New World screwworm is a parasitic fly larva that feeds on the living tissue of warm-blooded animals. Infestations can kill cattle, wildlife, and pets if untreated, making it one of the most serious livestock pests in the Western Hemisphere.

Mexico reported its first case to U.S. authorities in November 2024. As the parasite spread northward, USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins suspended live-animal imports through all southern border ports in May 2025, a ban that remained in place month by month while containment efforts ramped up.

Mexico’s eradication campaign has relied heavily on the sterile insect technique. Authorities are releasing more than 100 million sterile screwworm flies each week to collapse the wild population by preventing reproduction.

The Associated Press reported that by late July 2026, there had been no evidence of northward spread for eight consecutive weeks. That epidemiological pause gave USDA the confidence to begin the phased reopening.

At reopened ports, inspectors from USDA’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service will examine every shipment to ensure imported animals show no signs of screwworm infestation before they can enter U.S. territory.

Diplomatic Coordination Between Washington and Mexico City

Mexican Agriculture Secretary Julio Berdegué participated in a virtual meeting with USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins to confirm the restart. Berdegué had earlier signaled Mexico’s preference for a managed, phased return rather than an indefinite blanket closure.

The bilateral cooperation reflects the deep integration of the North American cattle market. Mexican authorities have pressed eradication measures including surveillance and sterile-fly dispersal to keep the outbreak from pushing further toward the U.S. border.

For Mexico, the closure created a glut of cattle that could not cross north, depressing domestic prices while U.S. ranchers and feedlots faced tighter supplies. The reopening, even if gradual, restores a critical export channel for Mexican producers.

What It Means for Cattle Prices

Industry analysts caution that the market impact of the reopening will likely be limited and gradual. There is no large backlog of animals waiting to move, and the phased schedule means supply will return in increments rather than a flood.

Brownfield Ag News quoted an analyst saying the restart would probably cause only a short-term, mostly psychological softening in feeder cattle prices. Any relief for U.S. buyers facing elevated input costs is expected to be temporary.

Reuters and The Wall Street Journal noted the reopening could help alleviate rising beef prices for American consumers, though the effect will take time to filter through the supply chain. The U.S.-Mexico cattle trade is substantial enough that prolonged disruption affects both supply and retail pricing.

For ranchers in states like Texas, where feedlots depend on Mexican feeder cattle, the reopening begins to restore a supply line that had been completely severed since May 2025. Mexican ranchers, meanwhile, regain access to the higher-paying U.S. market after more than a year of restricted options.

Looking Ahead: Conditions for Full Normalization

USDA has made clear that the pace of further reopenings depends entirely on continued progress against the screwworm. The department will monitor case numbers and geographic spread before greenlighting Santa Teresa and Columbus, and later the Texas crossings.

The sterile-fly campaign remains the cornerstone of containment. As long as Mexico sustains its weekly releases of over 100 million sterile flies and surveillance shows no renewed northward movement, the phased schedule can proceed.

For international investors and expatriates watching Latin American agricultural markets, the reopening signals that U.S. and Mexican authorities have found a workable balance between biosecurity and trade. The episode underscores how quickly a single pest can disrupt a multi-billion-dollar cross-border livestock economy.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did the US suspend Mexico cattle imports?

The USDA suspended live cattle imports from Mexico in May 2025 because of a northward-spreading outbreak of New World screwworm, a parasitic fly larva that feeds on living animal tissue and can kill livestock.

When will Mexico cattle imports fully resume?

Imports resume in phases starting August 24, 2026, at Douglas, Arizona. Santa Teresa and Columbus, New Mexico, will follow later, but no dates have been set for Texas ports like Del Rio and Laredo.

How will the reopening affect US beef prices?

Analysts expect only a limited, short-term psychological softening in feeder cattle prices. There is no large backlog of animals, and the phased reopening means supply returns gradually, so any consumer price relief will be modest and slow to materialize.

World.title: Alicorp Second Quarter Revenue Jumps 10.2%
World.content:
Peru · Companies

Key Facts —Q2 2026 Revenue S/3,155 million (~US$928 million), up 10.2% year-on-year —Q2 2026 Net Profit Above S/363 million (~US$107 million) —Q2 2026 Adjusted EBITDA S/470 million (~US$138 million), implying a 14.9% margin —International Sales Surge Jumped 58.7% to S/278 million (~US$82 million) after acquisitions —2026 Guidance Upgrade Revenue growth seen at mid-to-high single digits; EBITDA at lower-to-mid single digits

Alicorp second quarter results showed a 10.2% revenue jump to S/3,155 million (~US$928 million), as Peru’s largest consumer-goods maker benefited from recent acquisitions and steady domestic demand, prompting management to raise its full-year 2026 outlook.

Packaged foods on supermarket shelves; Alicorp is Peru’s largest consumer-goods maker. Photo: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA.

Alicorp Second Quarter Results

For foreign investors and expats, Alicorp S.A.A. is the largest mass-consumption company in Peru and a core holding of the powerful Romero Group, one of the country’s most influential family conglomerates. The Lima-based firm produces and distributes a vast portfolio of branded food, home-care, and personal-care products found in nearly every Peruvian household.

Beyond its domestic consumer brands, Alicorp runs a large business-to-business (B2B) operation selling industrial flour, oils, and shortenings, and controls Vitapro, a leading aquaculture feed and shrimp-farming unit with a growing footprint across Latin America. The company’s stock trades on the Lima Stock Exchange (BVL) under the ticker ALICORC1.

Sales Breakdown by Business Unit

The company’s Consumer Goods Peru division, its traditional profit engine, generated S/1,068 million (~US$314 million) in sales, an 11.2% increase from the same period last year. Management attributed the rise to stronger volumes and effective brand positioning in key categories.

The International segment delivered the most dramatic growth, with revenue soaring 58.7% to S/278 million (~US$82 million). The leap reflects the first full integration of Jabonería Wilson, a Bolivian home and personal-care company, and Inka Crops, a Peruvian snack exporter. Higher commercialized volumes in existing markets also contributed.

The B2B unit, which supplies industrial clients, posted a modest 2.0% revenue gain to S/795 million (~US$234 million). However, the division faced temporary pressure on profitability from commodity risk-management losses, a factor that partially offset the top-line increase.

Vitapro, the aquaculture and fish-feed business, recorded sales of S/1,013 million (~US$298 million), up 7.1% year-on-year. The unit continues to benefit from steady demand for shrimp feed in Ecuador and other regional markets, solidifying its role as a critical growth pillar outside of consumer packaged goods.

Profitability and Margins

Consolidated adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) reached S/470 million (~US$138 million) in the quarter. That figure implies an adjusted EBITDA margin of 14.9%, a healthy level for a diversified food and ingredients manufacturer.

Net income topped S/363 million (~US$107 million), though the exact final figure was not fully detailed in preliminary summaries. The B2B division specifically reported an adjusted EBITDA margin of 18.6%, underscoring the unit’s underlying operational efficiency despite the commodity-related headwinds.

Total sales volumes across the company rose 7.8% year-on-year, reaching 684,000 metric tons. The volume growth, combined with selective price adjustments, created a balanced mix that supported both revenue expansion and margin resilience.

Upgraded Full-Year Guidance

Alicorp’s management raised its 2026 forecast, now projecting mid- to high-single-digit revenue growth for the full year, up from a previously more cautious stance. The adjusted EBITDA outlook was also lifted to lower- to mid-single-digit growth, signaling confidence that the second-half operating environment will remain supportive.

The upgrade suggests that executives expect the integration benefits from Jabonería Wilson and Inka Crops to continue, while core Peruvian consumer demand stays firm. It also implies that the B2B unit’s risk-management losses are viewed as transitory rather than structural.

For international investors tracking Latin American consumer equities, the revised guidance positions Alicorp as a defensive yet growing play in a region where political noise often clouds the macroeconomic picture.

Context for Foreign Investors

Alicorp’s performance offers a window into Peruvian household consumption, which has proven resilient despite periodic political turmoil. The company’s brands – from cooking oils and detergents to pasta and cookies – are staples, making its revenue stream relatively stable.

The aggressive international push, particularly into Bolivia and the snack-export channel via Inka Crops, diversifies earnings away from the Peruvian sol. For dollar-based investors, this reduces some currency risk, though the primary listing remains in local currency.

With a market position comparable to a blend of Unilever and Bunge in a single entity, Alicorp remains a bellwether for Andean consumer markets. The second-quarter numbers reinforce a narrative of disciplined expansion and operational control.

Frequently Asked Questions

What were Alicorp’s total sales in the second quarter of 2026?

Alicorp reported consolidated net sales of S/3,155 million (~US$928 million) in Q2 2026, a 10.2% increase compared to the same quarter in 2025.

Why did Alicorp’s international sales jump so sharply?

International revenue surged 58.7% mainly due to the integration of recently acquired companies Jabonería Wilson in Bolivia and Inka Crops in Peru, along with higher commercialized volumes in existing markets.

What is Alicorp’s updated guidance for 2026?

Management raised its full-year 2026 outlook to mid- to high-single-digit revenue growth and lower- to mid-single-digit adjusted EBITDA growth, reflecting confidence in sustained demand and successful integration of acquisitions.

World.title: Ecuador Scientists Identify 8,000 New Insect Species
World.content:
Scientists in Ecuador announced Thursday that they had genetically identified 8,000 new insect species in a protected forest in the Ecuadorian Chocó Andino, a region designated as a World Biosphere Reserve. Researchers used genetic material from specimens collected in the private Mashpi-Tayra reserve, located northwest of Quito, and compared it with genetic information from other insects listed in scientific databases around the world.

Through this process, they determined that the specimens represented “new species,” said Diego Inclán, director of Ecuador’s National Institute of Biodiversity, known as Inabio. Ecuador is a small but megadiverse country. The study was published in the British scientific journal Scientific Data.

Of the 8,000 varieties, “97% are unique. They do not exist anywhere else on the planet. It is unbelievable,” Inclán said. The insects will now have to be described in detail and formally named through the traditional scientific process, he explained. After six years of research, including one year devoted exclusively to collecting specimens, scientists found that most of the previously unrecorded species were flies, wasps and butterflies.

“We used a new technology to describe species through their genetic fingerprint,” Inclán said. “A distinct genetic profile is equivalent to a species. The only difference is that it does not have a name; it has a code.” The research is part of an initiative led by the University of Guelph’s Centre for Biodiversity Genomics in Canada. The program includes 50 countries and studies how arthropod communities change over time and in response to environmental changes.

“These are extremely unique and already verified data. Hopefully, they will also help shape conservation policies at the local and national levels,” said Mateo Roldán, Mashpi’s research director. The Mashpi-Tayra protected forest covers about 3,200 hectares and lies within the Ecuadorian Chocó Andino, an area designated as a biosphere reserve eight years ago. The region has also been the focus of environmental campaigns seeking to stop mining activities.

The Mashpi research represents only one part of the broader project being carried out by Inabio, which is collecting flying insect specimens in other parts of the country. Inclán estimates that as genetic studies continue on the remaining samples collected in Mashpi, the number of reported insect species could double.

World.title: Costa Rican Stabbed in Manhattan Attack Investigated as Possible Hate Crime
World.content:
A Costa Rican citizen is among two men stabbed Thursday afternoon in a pair of attacks on Manhattan’s Upper West Side that New York police are investigating as a possible hate crime, Costa Rica’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed.

The Costa Rican, a 50-year-old man, was stabbed in the chest with a screwdriver near the corner of West 86th Street and Amsterdam Avenue shortly after 1:30 p.m., according to the New York Police Department. A short time earlier and roughly two blocks south, near West 84th Street and Central Park West, a 57-year-old man was stabbed in the back with a knife. Both men were taken to Mount Sinai Morningside Hospital in stable condition, and police said both are expected to survive.

In a statement posted to social media, Costa Rica’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Worship condemned the attack in the strongest terms, describing it as apparently motivated by ethnic and religious hatred and saying its citizen had been wounded because of his faith. The ministry expressed solidarity with everyone affected, singling out the injured compatriot and his family, and reiterated our country’s rejection of all forms of hatred, intolerance and violence.

It said it was providing support and consular assistance to the man, who according to the information available to authorities was in stable condition, and that it was monitoring the case through Costa Rica’s consular representation in the United States. Local reports indicated the man had been wearing a kipá, the head covering worn by observant Jewish men, and had recently attended observances for Tisha B’Av, a Jewish day of mourning, at a nearby center.

The New York Police Department arrested a 51-year-old man, whom it identified as Raúl Morales, in connection with both attacks. Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said victim and witness accounts indicated the suspect shouted “Allahu Akbar” during the assaults. Tisch said the department was evaluating whether the incidents amounted to a hate crime and noted that, while the suspect had no known mental health history with the NYPD, the early investigation suggested mental health may have been a factor. Officers took Morales into custody after he barricaded himself inside an apartment building near Amsterdam Avenue and West 88th Street, police said.

Morales was expected to appear before a judge on Friday, when prosecutors from the Manhattan District Attorney’s office were due to file formal charges that may differ from those initially brought by police. A law enforcement official told CNN that the charges are expected to include a hate crime count and attempted murder. The account of what took place remains preliminary, and authorities have cautioned that the investigation is in its early stages.

World.title: Costa Rica Captures Its Most Wanted Fugitive, After a Decade on the Run
World.content:
Costa Rican authorities detained Alejandro Arias Monge, the fugitive known as “Diablo,” early Friday morning in Sarapiquí, ending a manhunt that had run for nearly a decade and had drawn a half-million-dollar reward from the United States government. Attorney General Carlo Díaz confirmed the detention, which followed an armed confrontation between officers of the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ), and members of the criminal group protecting him.

The operation began shortly after 5 a.m. at a farm in the community of San Bernardino, in Río Frío de Sarapiquí, in the province of Heredia. Michael Soto, the OIJ’s interim director general, said agents from the agency’s Organized Crime Section and its Surveillance and Tracking Unit, supported by the Special Tactical Response Service and the Public Prosecutor’s Office, were met with gunfire as they entered the property. The exchange lasted approximately an hour. Soto described the intervention as a complex police operation and praised the conduct of the officers involved.

Five members of the Special Tactical Response Service, the OIJ’s tactical team, were wounded. According to the OIJ, four remained in stable condition and one was transferred to a medical center in San José for specialized care. The Costa Rican Red Cross gave a separate account of the evacuations, reporting that it moved four agents in advanced life support units, two classified as urgent and one in critical condition, while coordinating the air transfer of a fourth patient, also critical, to a hospital in the Greater Metropolitan Area. The two accounts differ on the severity of the injuries, and neither agency had issued a consolidated update at the time of writing.

Two other men considered senior figures in the organization were detained in the same operation. Jonathan Pérez Méndez, known as “Tan,” has been identified by the OIJ as Arias Monge’s presumed successor. Jorge David Núñez Aguilar, 31, known as “Coco Pastilla,” is considered the head of a group linked to the intellectual authorship of the killing of Geiner Zamora Hidalgo, the deputy chief of the OIJ’s Guápiles delegation, who was shot outside a restaurant in January 2025 and died days later. Núñez, a native of Pococí with a registered address in Guácimo, had been sought by the Judicial Police since that killing. A fourth suspect, identified by the surnames Ríos Oconitrillo and the alias “Coco Guácimo,” died during the operation after being shot by tactical officers, Soto said.

Agents seized five high-caliber rifles at the scene, including weapons of the AK-47 type, along with three pistols. Investigators also recovered drone equipment that the group is believed to have used to monitor the approaches to the property and complicate any police advance. Infobae reported that a FAL rifle was among the weapons recovered, a detail not carried by other outlets.

Arias Monge walked out of prison on October 28, 2016, after completing a period of preventive detention as a suspect in two homicide cases. He was subsequently declared in rebellion after failing to appear for trial, and his whereabouts remained unknown until Friday. Over the intervening years, authorities came to attribute to him as many as 100 killings, along with attempted homicides, drug trafficking, cattle theft and money laundering. The OIJ has also said he issued threats against police officers, including recordings in which he offered payment for the killing of agents. None of these allegations has been tested at trial, and the cases against him remain at the pre-trial stage.

Investigators had long placed him in the Guápiles area of Pococí, moving through rural terrain toward the northern border. Soto said in earlier interviews that Arias Monge relied on a small circle of people loyal to him to move undetected, and that the Judicial Police made more than ten attempts to detain him during 2024 alone. The Drug Enforcement Administration and Costa Rican authorities have identified cells operated by his network across all seven of the country’s provinces, with recent reporting placing its activity in the Caribbean, Sarapiquí, the northern zone, Pococí and Turrialba.

Soto has also cautioned that the figure of “Diablo” grew larger than the man. He has described the name functioning as a kind of franchise within criminal networks, used by others to frighten or extort victims, and has said a degree of mythology built up around him.

The case drew unusual attention from Washington. On April 30, 2025, the State Department’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs announced a reward of up to $500,000, roughly ₡250 million, under its Transnational Organized Crime Rewards Program, for information leading to the arrest or conviction of Arias Monge in any country. The offer, coordinated with the DEA, followed a series of meetings between the agency and Costa Rica’s Attorney General’s Office and OIJ. It is the largest reward the United States has offered for a Costa Rican national.

The State Department described him as the head of a violent transnational criminal organization and Costa Rica’s most wanted fugitive, wanted on multiple Costa Rican warrants for drug trafficking, robbery, aggravated homicide and money laundering. The DEA has said he conspired with traffickers to move multi-hundred-kilogram loads, or several hundred pounds, of cocaine from Colombia through Central America and Mexico toward the United States.

Speaking after the operation, Soto used the capture to argue for stronger funding for the judiciary, noting that his officers confronted an increasingly well-armed organization. The government of Laura Fernández announced in June a proposed reduction of ₡3.053 billion to the Judicial Branch’s 2026 budget, a cut the OIJ has said would constrain its capacity to carry out raids, conduct criminal analysis and protect victims.

Friday’s operation follows a sustained push against the network in recent weeks, including the July 9 detention of an alleged principal operator known as “Guato” in a mountainous area of Valle La Estrella. The OIJ said it would release further details in the coming hours on the circumstances of the detention and the condition of the wounded officers.

World.title: Costa Rica Flooding Closes 267 Schools as Sarapiquí Evacuations Climb
World.content:
If you live in Sarapiquí, Guápiles, Siquirres or the South Caribbean, today is not going to be a normal Friday. Schools are closed. Route 4 was cut through Sarapiquí. Hundreds of your neighbors slept in shelters. And the ground under all of it is holding about as much water as it can hold.

The Comisión Nacional de Emergencias (CNE) counted 800 people evacuated into nine shelters by late yesterday afternoon, according to CNE president Alejandro Picado. That figure is a running total of everyone pulled out of harm’s way, not a snapshot of who was still sheltered by nightfall.

Counts released earlier in the day ran lower and measured something different — more than 500 people in shelters at one point Thursday, and 348 people across six shelters in another CNE tally. The numbers move by the hour as families go home and new evacuations begin, so treat any single figure as a photograph rather than a measurement.

Picado named Sarapiquí as the hardest-hit canton. The communities sending the most people out are Naranjal 1, Naranjal 2, Carretones, Mortero, La Chave, El Palmar, Cureña and Cureñita. Firefighters and Red Cross crews used rafts and small boats to reach houses in El Tigre, Naranjales and El Nogal, where water covered the streets. The CNE delivered 1,250 food parcels and was arranging another 1,000, along with drinking water for households cut off from safe supply.

Your children are probably not in class today and depending on where you live that may have changed after you went to bed. The Ministerio de Educación Pública first suspended lessons Thursday and Friday at 157 schools — 138 in the Sarapiquí regional directorate, 14 in Guápiles and five in Siquirres, under the Limón directorate.

Late last night the ministry extended the suspension to all 110 schools in the Sulá regional directorate, which covers the South Caribbean. That brings the national total to 267 campuses closed. If your kids attend school anywhere between Bribri, Cahuita and Puerto Viejo de Talamanca, check the ministry’s official channels this morning rather than assuming yesterday’s list still applies.

The thing worth understanding today is why ordinary rain is now doing extraordinary damage. The Instituto Meteorológico Nacional reported Thursday that river basins across the Caribbean, the Northern Zone and the South Pacific are sitting near 95 percent saturation. Soil that full behaves like a paved parking lot.

Rain that would normally soak in instead runs straight off the hillside and into the nearest quebrada, which is why a moderate afternoon downpour can now push a river over its banks in under an hour. The IMN measured 20 to 50 millimeters (0.8 to 2 inches) of rain Thursday morning alone, with peaks of 60 to 85 millimeters (2.4 to 3.3 inches) around Horquetas, Sarapiquí, Montaña Sagrada, Pococí and Cariari. Overnight Wednesday into Thursday, Canta Gallo de Limón took 81.8 millimeters (3.2 inches) and Sarapiquí 44.2 millimeters (1.7 inches).

There is a second, less obvious risk on the Río Sarapiquí. Emergency crews spent yesterday verifying whether a landslide has formed a plug in the river channel. A plug like that acts as an accidental dam. It holds water back, the level builds behind it, and then it fails all at once — sending a surge downstream with almost no warning to anyone below it. That is the specific scenario the CNE is watching, and it is the reason to take an evacuation instruction seriously even if the river in front of your house looks calm at the moment you receive it.

Roads are the other daily problem. Route 4 was blocked in Sarapiquí on Thursday, and Route 32 over the Zurquí has closed repeatedly this month when material comes down on the carriageway. Confirm the status with the MOPT before you commit to a drive, because the alternates are slower than they look on a map: Vara Blanca handles light vehicles only, and Bajos de Chilamate–Vuelta Kooper takes any vehicle but adds real time. If you reach standing water on a road, turn around. You cannot see whether the roadbed underneath has washed out, and moving water pushes a vehicle sideways long before the water reaches the door.

Travelers should build slack into today. The overland route to Tortuguero runs Guápiles to Cariari to the La Pavona dock, straight through the affected corridor, and the same weather that closed schools can close a boat schedule. Lodges in Sarapiquí, La Selva and the Puerto Viejo de Sarapiquí area are inside the flood footprint. Call ahead rather than driving out and finding out. In Talamanca, rising rivers damaged dikes, roads and homes, and the CNE delivered aid to 50 fishing families in Puerto Viejo, Punta Uva and Manzanillo who could not get out on the water.

The forecast offers a partial break and then takes it back. The IMN expects a warmer, brighter morning as cloud cover thins, but an active Intertropical Convergence Zone and a hit of humidity moving in off the Caribbean should rebuild rain through the afternoon and into the night.

The North Caribbean starts cloudy with drizzle and intermittent rain and keeps a chance of showers all day, with Guápiles between 22.4 and 28 degrees Celsius (72 to 82 Fahrenheit). The South Caribbean follows the same pattern. Do not read a dry morning as the end of this. The IMN expects tropical wave No. 25 to reach the country on Sunday, landing on ground that will have had no time to drain.

The yellow alert stands for the Northern Zone, the north and south Caribbean, and the canton of Turrialba. If you are in those areas, keep your phone charged, keep documents and medication somewhere you can grab in one motion, and go when the municipal emergency committee tells you to go. Emergencies go to 9-1-1.

World.title: Electric Cars in Costa Rica Face a Higher Sales Tax
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Finance Ministry has increased the selective consumption tax applied to electric vehicles, a change Finance Minister Rodrigo Chaves announced Wednesday evening and which the country’s electric mobility industry says was already mandated by legislation approved four years ago.

Chaves, who also serves as Minister of the Presidency, said in a television interview that he had signed the decree that day. He gave two figures in the course of his remarks. He said electric vehicles had been paying a 6% rate and that the government intends to bring that figure to 30%, and he said separately that the rate applied immediately is 7.5%.

The minister defended the measure on the grounds that Costa Rica’s potential contribution to combating climate change is minimal. He questioned the electric vehicle incentive policies pursued by previous administrations and said the country should concentrate its resources on measures that produce direct benefits.

Silvia Rojas, director of the Costa Rican Electric Mobility Association, known by its Spanish acronym Asomove, disputed the characterization of the change as a government initiative. She said the 2022 reform to the Green Transport Incentives Law had already established that electric vehicles would begin paying 25% of the full 30% selective consumption rate, the figure of 7.5% that Chaves announced, and that the schedule called for that step to take effect last year rather than this week.

“The announcement is not about new taxes,” Rojas said, describing the decree instead as the law being carried out as written. Rojas also set out the remaining schedule the legislation establishes. By 2028, electric vehicles would pay half the selective consumption rate, equivalent to 15 percentage points of the 30. By 2031 the proportion rises to three quarters, or 22.5 points.

In 2034, the full 30% applies. The same law governs reduced value added tax and customs valuation rates for electric vehicles alongside the selective consumption levy. The minister did not address how vehicles already imported or awaiting customs clearance will be treated, and publication of the decree in La Gaceta, the official gazette, has not been confirmed.

Electric vehicle registrations have been rising steadily. Figures compiled by Asomove recorded 1,064 new electric vehicles registered in April 2026 alone, of which 1,007 were passenger cars, with the remainder made up of motorcycles, specialised vehicles and work vehicles.

The decree emerged from a wider fiscal package the Finance Ministry presented Wednesday, comprising more than 15 bills covering electronic invoicing, penalties for tax evasion, the regulation of exemptions and a reform of income tax. Chaves has said the government does not intend to create new taxes, and the ministry has indicated that applying the 13% value added tax to the basic food basket remains under consideration, subject to conditions.

Chaves said in the same interview that the ministry will file a separate bill in September to simplify and reduce the taxes levied on alcohol and cigarettes. He did not specify the size of the proposed reduction, saying only that the initiative would cover both categories.

World.title: October court date set for Elvira Mulholland; accused of attempting to murder her husband
World.content:
October court date set for Elvira Mulholland; accused of attempting to murder her husband

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A tentative October 2, 2026 court date has been set in the attempted murder case against Elvira Mulholland, who is accused of shooting her husband during a domestic dispute in 2024.

Mulholland appeared before Justice Candace Nanton in the High Court on Friday, represented by attorney Dr. Lynden Jones. She remains out on High Court bail.

The defence informed the court that Mulholland is also currently on trial in the Magistrate’s Court for an alleged robbery arising from the same incident. That trial, which began in April, is scheduled to continue on August 3.

Justice Nanton adjourned the attempted murder matter until October 2 for a case management conference, by which time the lower court proceedings are expected to have concluded. A firm trial date could then be determined.

Police allege that on October 25, 2024, Mulholland followed her husband, Jeffrey Mulholland, along the Coastal Road, ran his pickup truck off the road and shot him with his own licensed firearm following a struggle.

She was committed to stand trial in the High Court after a preliminary inquiry concluded in July 2025.

World.title: Collin Francis found stable to stand trial for murder of Nestor Vasquez Jr. but Court says it won’t accept just one evaluation
World.content:
Collin Francis found stable to stand trial for murder of Nestor Vasquez Jr. but Court says it won’t accept just one evaluation

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The murder case against Collin Francis Jr. could take a significant turn when it returns to the High Court on Tuesday, July 28, 2026.

Francis had previously been found unfit to enter a plea and was ordered to undergo psychiatric evaluations every six months for two years. However, Justice Nigel Pilgrim was informed on Friday that only one evaluation had been completed.

The June 29, 2026 report, prepared by psychiatrist Dr. Denethia Usher, found that Francis is now stable, taking his medication and considered fit to enter a plea. The report also noted that his condition had improved while he was away from marijuana.

The prosecution indicated that the Director of Public Prosecutions’ office was prepared to proceed to trial. Justice Pilgrim, however, said he would not allow the case to proceed to trial based solely on the single evaluation.

The judge asked whether the prosecution would consider accepting a guilty plea, but the Crown said instructions would first have to be obtained from the DPP.

Francis is charged with the 2019 murder of 60-year-old Nestor Vasquez Jr., who was fatally injured while the two men were detained in a cell at the Queen Street Police Station.

The matter was adjourned until Tuesday for the prosecution to indicate how it intends to proceed.

World.title: BDF volunteer soldier Mark Nolberto sentenced to nearly 18 Years for raping 17-year-old girl and videoing it; Says his sentence is ‘unjust’
World.content:
BDF volunteer soldier Mark Nolberto sentenced to nearly 18 Years for raping 17-year-old girl and videoing it; Says his sentence is ‘unjust’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: High Court Justice Candace Nanton today sentenced 31-year-old Belize Defence Force (BDF) volunteer soldier Mark Anthony Nolberto to 17 years, 10 months, and 3 weeks in prison following his conviction on two counts of rape against a 17-year-old girl.

Justice Nanton ordered that the sentences for both counts run concurrently. In addition to his prison term, Nolberto must undergo counseling as well as medical and psychiatric treatment while incarcerated.
