World.title: Swans turn Giants into punching bag in Sydney Derby demolition
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Swans turn Giants into punching bag in Sydney Derby demolition Jonathan Drennan July 25, 2026 — 7:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Over 14 years of the Sydney Derby, the Giants had worked tirelessly to become a feared opponent for the Swans, but in their 33rd meeting, they were reduced to a punching bag for their city rivals, losing by 51 points. Swans forward Charlie Curnow kicked four goals to underline his Coleman Medal credentials and Errol Gulden finished with 41 disposals to help his team overrun a desperately overmatched Giants midfield. Giants star Finn Callaghan also left the field in the final quarter limping after a lower leg injury. Errol Gulden of the Swans runs with the ball. Getty Images GWS endured a disastrous first half and not only due to entering the dressing room 53 points down against their fiercest rivals. The Giants’ total of 18 tackles in the first half highlighted an inability to pressurise the Swans, with the notable exception of Giants veteran Stephen Coniglio and midfielder Clayton Oliver, who refused to give up throughout the game.



The Swans will now look to hold on to second place on the AFL ladder, while the Giants will be left with far more questions than answers in their quest to play finals football. The Giants defeated Fremantle, Brisbane, Hawthorn and Geelong this season. Their best is sublime, while their worst was on display against the Swans. The Giants were without their talismanic captain Toby Greene due to a quad strain. He was dearly missed not only for his brilliance as a player but also as a unique leader capable of sparking a response from his teammates at the toughest times. Charlie Curnow celebrates a goal against the Giants Getty Images Greene’s old sparring partner Tom Papley’s first goal was met with an unusually muted celebration, responding to the lack of pressure faced by the Giants and perhaps the absence of Greene. Greene played the first Sydney Derby in 2012, when the Giants lost by 63 points, alongside Stephen Coniglio. Despite the heavy loss, the youthful team could not have been accused of lacking heart or appetite. On Saturday evening, that foundation that was so painfully built crumbled.



Swans midfielder Braeden Campbell had missed the majority of this season due to a shin stress fracture. In just his second game of the year, Campbell returned to form, with his newly bleached blonde hair spotted all over Engie Stadium in the first quarter. Campbell kicked the first goal in under a minute, benefiting from his team’s slick passing movement. Tom Papley celebrates for the Swans Getty Images Curnow had kicked goals in 11 straight games but was held goalless in the loss against Adelaide last Friday. Against the Giants the drought ended emphatically, with Curnow kicking two in the first quarter. James Rowbottom and Jai Serong added their first majors of the afternoon to open up a 30-point lead. Xavier O’Halloran’s first goal for the Giants wasn’t met with a cheer from Engie Stadium so much as a collective sigh of relief. It was short-lived.



Goals for Papley and Brodie Grundy extended the lead to 37 points with their first majors. Chad Warner kicked his first goal from a tight angle from the boundary line to start the second quarter. Warner thrives in space and the Giants gifted him lots of it. Curnow gifted the Giants with a 100-metre penalty thanks to ruffling Clayton Oliver’s hair. Jayden Laverde had a chance to kick a major 20 metres directly in front of goal. Laverde hit the post. It summed up the Giants’ day. Then the Swans’ Billy Cootee’s goal extended the lead to 45 points. Coniglio’s second goal of the game provided some rare resistance for the home side, alongside Clayton Oliver who was fighting a difficult battle in the midfield almost alone. Curnow and Cootee kicked their third and second goals respectively, contrasting with Logan McDonald, who 20 minutes into the second quarter had not registered a single disposal, tackle or mark on the field.



Giants coach Adam Kingsley looked intently at his laptop with his side 53 points down with McDonald finally getting a goal. The Giants desperately needed a response after heading into the dressing room 53 points down and they finally got it at the start of the third quarter. Coniglio spoke of his desire to finish his career at the Giants and his third goal at the start of the third quarter will have done his ongoing negotiations no harm. Giants midfielder Ryan Angwin also kicked two majors for the quarter to try to spark a response from his team, but it proved in vain. Curnow’s fourth major and Logan McDonald’s third goal kept the Giants comfortably at bay. Hayden McLean’s first goal of the game extended the margin to a game-high 59 points.



The final quarter provided some of the Giants’ best work, with successive goals to Jake Stringer and Joe Fonti, but it was far too little too late. The Swans were able to treat the closing stages like a training ground drill, Jake Lloyd, James Rowbottom and Isaac Heeney kicking majors to underline a comfortable victory that could have and should have been far greater. A fire alarm went off in the stadium towards the end of the game, recommending an evacuation. The Giants had seemingly heeded the warning far earlier in the game against an opposition that normally brings out the very best in them.

World.title: How a tug-of-war over a ‘handsome mayor’ may shape the political fortunes of the Nationals
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election How a tug-of-war over a ‘handsome mayor’ may shape the political fortunes of the Nationals Chip Le Grand July 25, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An unexpected decision by Nationals MP Kim O’Keeffe to vacate her seat of Shepparton before the November election has abruptly transformed the Goulburn Valley electorate into one of the state’s most fascinating political contests. It is a race thus far without a declared candidate for any of the three parties in the hunt for the seat – the Nationals, the Liberal Party and One Nation – and all have their eyes on the same potential recruit, City of Shepparton Mayor Shane Sali. Nationals MP Kim O’Keeffe won’t be re-contesting the seat of Shepparton. Nationals leader Danny O’Brien said the loss of O’Keeffe, herself a former local mayor who in 2022 regained Shepparton from two-term independent Suzanna Sheed, would make more challenging his party’s already difficult job to defend the seat. It leaves the Nationals having to cover for retiring members in three of their nine lower house seats – Shepparton, Murray Plains and Gippsland East — and without the benefit of incumbency in trying to hold back the orange tide in electorates vulnerable to Pauline Hanson’s populism.



Murray Plains, Shepparton and Benambra – a Liberal-held seat where long-serving MP Bill Tilley is retiring due to ill health – all look across the Murray River to the NSW federal electorate of Farrer where, just two months ago, One Nation wiped out the Coalition partners in a by-election mauling. “It is always a bit harder when you have got a retiring member and trying to transition a seat, but we are confident we will get a strong, local champion again, like we did with Kim, and fight hard to win every vote,” O’Brien said. “We don’t shy away from the fact there will be a strong contest. There always is. There is no such thing as a safe seat anymore and that has probably been the case for the Nats for longer than anyone else.” O’Keeffe campaigned in Shepparton with O’Brien and Opposition Leader Jess Wilson just two weeks ago but then announced she would not recontest her seat. “The time has come for me to slow down, spend more time with my family, and some much-needed self-care,” she said in a statement posted on her website this week.



O’Keeffe declined to expand on her reasons when contacted by this masthead. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Jess Wilson is trying to convince Victoria to trust her party, one High Street at a time The success of the Nationals in winning back regional seats from independents in Shepparton, Mildura and Morwell at the last state election, when added to the personal electoral brand of some of their longer serving MPs, is a potential bulwark against One Nation in Victoria. Redbridge director Kos Samaras, whose polling company has done seat-by-seat modelling for the state election for the Victorian Trades Hall Council, is cautious when projecting losses from the Nationals to One Nation. “One Nation needs an extraordinarily high primary vote to win,” Samaras said. “Against an incumbent, popular, National Party MP, that is going to be very difficult. Where a seat is vacant is where you will see One Nation take its gains.”



Shepparton Mayor Shane Sali is hot property as a potential candidate. The exception to this rule, Samaras says, is the Latrobe Valley seat of Morwell, which he describes as “ground zero” for One Nation in Victoria. In Shepparton, the most pressing question is the political future of Sali, a councillor known locally as the “handsome mayor” and familiar to Today Show audiences. He is mooted as a potential candidate for the Nationals but his family, one of the region’s celebrated migrant stories, has strong links to the Liberals. One Nation is understood to have Sali on their wish-list of candidates but his fellow councillor, Steve Threlfall, a well known local shooting and sporting goods store owner, confirmed on Thursday he was also interested in representing Hanson’s party. “I’m certainly chasing pre-selection,” Threlfall said. One Nation’s sole representative in the Victorian parliament, upper house MP Rikkie-Lee Tyrrell, has her electorate office in Shepparton.



Sali, when contacted by this masthead, paid tribute to O’Keeffe’s contribution to the region as a state MP and local councillor but declined to canvass his political options. “I’m the current Mayor, I’m not a member of any political party and my focus has always been the outcomes that our community is trying to achieve,” he said. He added that, irrespective of who next represents Shepparton, there is broad consensus about what the regional centre needs – better roads, more frequent train services, an expanded sports and events centre, and a second crossing over the Goulburn River to stop heavy trucks from rumbling along the existing causeway through the centre of Mooroopna and Shepparton. Shepparton is Victoria’s only major regional centre without an integrated cancer centre at its local hospital. The closure of the Bega Cheese factory at the end of last month – with the loss of more than 300 jobs – crystallised regional insecurities about the combined impact of water buy-backs under the revised Murray Darling Basin Plan and rising gas prices on agriculture, horticulture and food manufacturing.



Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election An orange wave is breaking over Victoria. Can Labor hold back the populist tide? Linda Nieuwenhuizen, the chief executive of the Committee for Greater Shepparton, said the recent political history of the region suggested voters were less guided by party loyalty than a yearning for practical outcomes. “We want to see the next government have a real ambition for what regions like ours can deliver,” she said. “We are a big food manufacturing and production centre. We know there is global growth happening that we want to be a part of.” Sheed, who represented Shepparton between 2014 and 2022 and is not planning to run again, said there was a lot of hype about One Nation and a level of voter frustration she didn’t encounter when she entered state politics. “It feels angrier now than then,” she said. “The major parties need to accept that One Nation’s rise is not just an electoral challenge or a political problem. It’s the result of historic and ongoing policy failings. The remedy, therefore, must be better policy”. World.title: The two factors that cut $450 from your household’s monthly budget
World.content:
Exclusive BusinessThe economySpending The two factors that cut $450 from your household’s monthly budget Matt Wade July 25, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Soaring petrol prices and multiple interest rate hikes have delivered the biggest quarterly hit to household finances in more than two decades. The spending power of families with a mortgage and two cars was slashed by an average of $450 per month in the March quarter this year, while non-essential funds available to a typical renter couple fell by $180 per month. Households that own their home outright were the least affected, with a drop in non-essential funds of $140 a month. Households have faced the steepest hit to their budgets in over two decades. Louie Douvis A report that tracks household finances by economic consultancy Polis Partners shows the first three months of 2026 saw the sharpest quarterly fall in discretionary household income since the series began in 2004. During that period, the Reserve Bank lifted interest rates twice and petrol prices surged above $2.50 a litre following attacks by the US and Israel on Iran in late February.



That financial double blow erased almost all the recovery that the average household made to their budgets over 2024 and 2025, leaving them “back where they were 15 years ago in real terms”, the study said. The Reserve Bank also lifted interest in May, but the effects of that decision were not included in the study. Polis Partners director Rob Tyson said this year has shown how quickly household budgets can deteriorate when multiple cost pressures arrive at the same time. “There’s been a big jump in what households have to devote to essentials and that leaves an awful lot less to spend on other things,” he said.



But the impact has been uneven. “Housing circumstances, household composition and income all shape how exposed a family is,” Tyson said. “A couple with a mortgage and two petrol cars they rely on to run the kids around and commute to work were really hit hard, whereas a self-funded retiree couple who have paid off the house and drive an EV have been largely insulated from the shock.” The lowest 20 per cent of income earners have been disproportionately affected; for those households essential costs exceed income by about $81 a week on average, meaning they must draw on saving or use credit to make ends meet.



Households with middle and lower-middle incomes have seen a significant fall in the amount of discretionary funds available to spend. But high-income households, especially those who own their homes outright, have been relatively insulated from the cost-of-living squeeze. Over the whole year to March 2026, the amount the average household had to spend on non-essential items fell by $782. Tyson warns there may be more pain in sight for Australian households. “Unfortunately, the squeeze isn’t over,” he said.

World.content:
Another gutsy win for Canterbury tonight, winning 18-6 after starting underdogs against a quality team.

The Bulldogs’ built their strong 2025 campaign on defence and they have shown more of that in the past fortnight, conceding just one try across two games, and had some quality flashes of attack as well tonight, particularly from back-rowers Viliame Kikau and Jacob Preston.

World.title: There’s more than mythology to Australia’s most hyped new rock band
World.content:
CultureMusicReview There’s more than mythology to Australia’s most hyped new rock band Jules LeFevre and and Robert Moran July 25, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Swapmeet, Mount Zero ★★★ Mount Zero by Swapmeet: a remarkably focused debut. “Mount Zero is a place you pass but never go,” Swapmeet’s Maxwell Elphick says of the mountain that looms as the northernmost point of the Grampians. The band would pass by the cryptically named mountain again and again while journeying from their hometown of Adelaide to Melbourne to play gigs.



These long, empty road trips have become part of the much-hyped indie rock group’s mythology – their first-ever show in Wollongong was packed full of devoted Adelaideans who’d made the trip across the border in support. It’s appropriate, then, that their debut album stretches and turns like one of these trips. There’s the propulsive thud of single and opener I Know!, the messy dirge of Seeds and the breeziness of standout Sand, while smatterings of horns and shrieking guitars slap exclamation marks on Personal (Don’t Take it) and Halfway. Local breakout indie-rockers Swapmeet. Josh Sabini Band members Maxwell Elphick, Venus O’Broin, Jack Medlyn and Josh Doherty swap instruments and vocals throughout the album, which they pieced together in a Port Noarlunga pad that had a ping-pong table overlooking the ocean. Despite the musical chairs, Mount Zero is a remarkably focused and even debut album, with its icy atmosphere recalling ’90s alt-rock – and a solitary drive on an empty highway. Jules LeFevre



Frost Children, Tweaker Poem ★★★★ Tweaker Poem by Frost Children: anthemic EDM at its serrated best. NYC-via-Midwest sibling duo Lulu and Angel Prost have seen their star rise exponentially since last year’s Sister, their sixth album in as many years, and their production work with the likes of Kim Petras and Ninajirachi. With that increasing profile has come a major label record deal and unwanted attention of the parasocial kind. Following an encounter with an overzealous fan (the EP’s eponymous “tweaker”), the duo fled New York and decamped to Tokyo, where – jet-lagged and sleep-deprived – they recorded this EP inspired by the entire ordeal. In songs that quote Madonna’s stalker Robert Dewey Hoskins and Rhonda Saunders’ book Whisper of Fear: the True Story of the Prosecutor Who Stalks the Stalkers, the pair scrutinise the encounter with emotional detail.



The result, somehow, isn’t dark or dour but life-affirming and warm, veering away from the brash indie sleaze they’re known for and further towards the pop aspirations and melodic melancholy that marked the best parts of Sister. Sibling duo Lulu and Angel Prost are Frost Children. Satellites and Light Leak match their hyperpop experimentalism with the sort of chart-topping emo-EDM that poured out of dorm rooms in the mid-2010s (think the Chainsmokers, Zedd, et al.), while the sparkling synths and serrated choruses of Creep and Afterlife lie somewhere between Dance Dance Revolution and Midwest emo. You’ll find yourself euphorically chanting “We never die, ain’t no cyanide!” over a frantic gabber beat like it’s a mantra. Robert Moran To read more from Spectrum, visit our page here. World.title: ‘Terrifying attack’: Accused rapist allegedly ambushed woman working from home
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts ‘Terrifying attack’: Accused rapist allegedly ambushed woman working from home Eleanor Campbell July 25, 2026 — 6:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A man accused of forcing himself into a woman’s home and threatening her with a knife before raping her on a kitchen floor has denied a string of sexual assaults in Melbourne’s outer west, including another case at a nearby school the following day. Timothy Richards, 39, appeared in Melbourne Magistrates Court on Saturday after being charged with two counts of rape, one count of aggravated burglary and one count of threats to kill. Police outside the scene of one of the alleged sexual assaults in Hoppers Crossing. Nine News Police allege he knocked on the door of a house on Whitsunday Drive, in Hoppers Crossing, on Thursday while the woman was alone and working from home. The court heard he had been living at an ex-partner’s house nearby and had approached the property 20 minutes earlier where the pair had engaged in a brief conversation.



Richards then allegedly produced a large kitchen knife and threatened to kill the 35-year-old woman before ordering her to remove her clothes as she screamed and pleaded with him to leave. The court heard the man, who police say was wearing a hoodie and had his face covered to conceal his identity, refused and grabbed her jacket, before dragging the woman into a nearby kitchen and sexually assaulting her. Loading It is alleged he then pushed the woman to the ground and raped her before getting up and walking out the front door. The woman told investigators she eventually got up and locked the door and called her husband when she realised he had left.



Sexual crimes squad detective Aiden Verdun described the alleged assault as a “terrifying attack on a vulnerable victim in the safety of her own home”. Richards has also been accused of another alleged sexual assault on Friday, when a woman was approached outside Mossfiel Primary School, in Langridge Street, Hoppers Crossing, about 6.45am. Police allege the woman, who was a staff member, was outside collecting bins when a man wearing a high-vis vest attempted to engage in a conversation with her before following her into a nearby classroom. The court heard the man placed the woman in a headlock as she fought and attempted to kick him off before he allegedly raped her. Detectives are also investigating a third incident where a 21-year-old woman was followed and grabbed at a nearby bus stop.



The woman recalled the man as being about six feet tall and of South-East Asian appearance. Investigators are trying to establish through DNA testing if the Hoppers Crossing incidents are linked. Richards, who denies all the allegations against him, was arrested on Friday morning. The court heard he was on bail for three separate matters, including charges of unlawful assault, assault with a weapon, criminal damage, and possession of methamphetamine. He appeared during a court hearing on Saturday afternoon with his shaved head down.



He will be remanded in custody and appear before a court on November 27. Police also attended a house in nearby Branton Road in Hoppers Crossing after a resident reported a possible burglary overnight Friday. The 39-year-old man will return to Melbourne Magistrates Court in October. With Ashleigh McMillan

Charlie Curnow celebrates a goal against the Giants Getty Images Greene’s old sparring partner Tom Papley’s first goal was met with an unusually muted celebration, responding to the lack of pressure faced by the Giants and perhaps the absence of Greene. Greene played the first Sydney Derby in 2012, when the Giants lost by 63 points, alongside Stephen Coniglio. Despite the heavy loss, the youthful team could not have been accused of lacking heart or appetite. On Saturday evening, that foundation that was so painfully built crumbled.



Swans midfielder Braeden Campbell had missed the majority of this season due to a shin stress fracture. In just his second game of the year, Campbell returned to form, with his newly bleached blonde hair spotted all over Engie Stadium in the first quarter. Campbell kicked the first goal in under a minute, benefiting from his team’s slick passing movement. Tom Papley celebrates for the Swans Getty Images Curnow had kicked goals in 11 straight games but was held goalless in the loss against Adelaide last Friday. Against the Giants the drought ended emphatically, with Curnow kicking two in the first quarter. James Rowbottom and Jai Serong added their first majors of the afternoon to open up a 30-point lead. Xavier O’Halloran’s first goal for the Giants wasn’t met with a cheer from Engie Stadium so much as a collective sigh of relief. It was short-lived.



Goals for Papley and Brodie Grundy extended the lead to 37 points with their first majors. Chad Warner kicked his first goal from a tight angle from the boundary line to start the second quarter. Warner thrives in space and the Giants gifted him lots of it. Curnow gifted the Giants with a 100-metre penalty thanks to ruffling Clayton Oliver’s hair. Jayden Laverde had a chance to kick a major 20 metres directly in front of goal. Laverde hit the post. It summed up the Giants’ day. Then the Swans’ Billy Cootee’s goal extended the lead to 45 points. Coniglio’s second goal of the game provided some rare resistance for the home side, alongside Clayton Oliver who was fighting a difficult battle in the midfield almost alone. Curnow and Cootee kicked their third and second goals respectively, contrasting with Logan McDonald, who 20 minutes into the second quarter had not registered a single disposal, tackle or mark on the field.



Giants coach Adam Kingsley looked intently at his laptop with his side 53 points down with McDonald finally getting a goal. The Giants desperately needed a response after heading into the dressing room 53 points down and they finally got it at the start of the third quarter. Coniglio spoke of his desire to finish his career at the Giants and his third goal at the start of the third quarter will have done his ongoing negotiations no harm. Giants midfielder Ryan Angwin also kicked two majors for the quarter to try to spark a response from his team, but it proved in vain. Curnow’s fourth major and Logan McDonald’s third goal kept the Giants comfortably at bay. Hayden McLean’s first goal of the game extended the margin to a game-high 59 points.



The final quarter provided some of the Giants’ best work, with successive goals to Jake Stringer and Joe Fonti, but it was far too little too late. The Swans were able to treat the closing stages like a training ground drill, Jake Lloyd, James Rowbottom and Isaac Heeney kicking majors to underline a comfortable victory that could have and should have been far greater. A fire alarm went off in the stadium towards the end of the game, recommending an evacuation. The Giants had seemingly heeded the warning far earlier in the game against an opposition that normally brings out the very best in them.

World.title: How a tug-of-war over a ‘handsome mayor’ may shape the political fortunes of the Nationals
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election How a tug-of-war over a ‘handsome mayor’ may shape the political fortunes of the Nationals Chip Le Grand July 25, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An unexpected decision by Nationals MP Kim O’Keeffe to vacate her seat of Shepparton before the November election has abruptly transformed the Goulburn Valley electorate into one of the state’s most fascinating political contests. It is a race thus far without a declared candidate for any of the three parties in the hunt for the seat – the Nationals, the Liberal Party and One Nation – and all have their eyes on the same potential recruit, City of Shepparton Mayor Shane Sali. Nationals MP Kim O’Keeffe won’t be re-contesting the seat of Shepparton. Nationals leader Danny O’Brien said the loss of O’Keeffe, herself a former local mayor who in 2022 regained Shepparton from two-term independent Suzanna Sheed, would make more challenging his party’s already difficult job to defend the seat. It leaves the Nationals having to cover for retiring members in three of their nine lower house seats – Shepparton, Murray Plains and Gippsland East — and without the benefit of incumbency in trying to hold back the orange tide in electorates vulnerable to Pauline Hanson’s populism.



Murray Plains, Shepparton and Benambra – a Liberal-held seat where long-serving MP Bill Tilley is retiring due to ill health – all look across the Murray River to the NSW federal electorate of Farrer where, just two months ago, One Nation wiped out the Coalition partners in a by-election mauling. “It is always a bit harder when you have got a retiring member and trying to transition a seat, but we are confident we will get a strong, local champion again, like we did with Kim, and fight hard to win every vote,” O’Brien said. “We don’t shy away from the fact there will be a strong contest. There always is. There is no such thing as a safe seat anymore and that has probably been the case for the Nats for longer than anyone else.” O’Keeffe campaigned in Shepparton with O’Brien and Opposition Leader Jess Wilson just two weeks ago but then announced she would not recontest her seat. “The time has come for me to slow down, spend more time with my family, and some much-needed self-care,” she said in a statement posted on her website this week.



O’Keeffe declined to expand on her reasons when contacted by this masthead. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Jess Wilson is trying to convince Victoria to trust her party, one High Street at a time The success of the Nationals in winning back regional seats from independents in Shepparton, Mildura and Morwell at the last state election, when added to the personal electoral brand of some of their longer serving MPs, is a potential bulwark against One Nation in Victoria. Redbridge director Kos Samaras, whose polling company has done seat-by-seat modelling for the state election for the Victorian Trades Hall Council, is cautious when projecting losses from the Nationals to One Nation. “One Nation needs an extraordinarily high primary vote to win,” Samaras said. “Against an incumbent, popular, National Party MP, that is going to be very difficult. Where a seat is vacant is where you will see One Nation take its gains.”



Shepparton Mayor Shane Sali is hot property as a potential candidate. The exception to this rule, Samaras says, is the Latrobe Valley seat of Morwell, which he describes as “ground zero” for One Nation in Victoria. In Shepparton, the most pressing question is the political future of Sali, a councillor known locally as the “handsome mayor” and familiar to Today Show audiences. He is mooted as a potential candidate for the Nationals but his family, one of the region’s celebrated migrant stories, has strong links to the Liberals. One Nation is understood to have Sali on their wish-list of candidates but his fellow councillor, Steve Threlfall, a well known local shooting and sporting goods store owner, confirmed on Thursday he was also interested in representing Hanson’s party. “I’m certainly chasing pre-selection,” Threlfall said. One Nation’s sole representative in the Victorian parliament, upper house MP Rikkie-Lee Tyrrell, has her electorate office in Shepparton.



Sali, when contacted by this masthead, paid tribute to O’Keeffe’s contribution to the region as a state MP and local councillor but declined to canvass his political options. “I’m the current Mayor, I’m not a member of any political party and my focus has always been the outcomes that our community is trying to achieve,” he said. He added that, irrespective of who next represents Shepparton, there is broad consensus about what the regional centre needs – better roads, more frequent train services, an expanded sports and events centre, and a second crossing over the Goulburn River to stop heavy trucks from rumbling along the existing causeway through the centre of Mooroopna and Shepparton. Shepparton is Victoria’s only major regional centre without an integrated cancer centre at its local hospital. The closure of the Bega Cheese factory at the end of last month – with the loss of more than 300 jobs – crystallised regional insecurities about the combined impact of water buy-backs under the revised Murray Darling Basin Plan and rising gas prices on agriculture, horticulture and food manufacturing.



Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election An orange wave is breaking over Victoria. Can Labor hold back the populist tide? Linda Nieuwenhuizen, the chief executive of the Committee for Greater Shepparton, said the recent political history of the region suggested voters were less guided by party loyalty than a yearning for practical outcomes. “We want to see the next government have a real ambition for what regions like ours can deliver,” she said. “We are a big food manufacturing and production centre. We know there is global growth happening that we want to be a part of.” Sheed, who represented Shepparton between 2014 and 2022 and is not planning to run again, said there was a lot of hype about One Nation and a level of voter frustration she didn’t encounter when she entered state politics. “It feels angrier now than then,” she said. “The major parties need to accept that One Nation’s rise is not just an electoral challenge or a political problem. It’s the result of historic and ongoing policy failings. The remedy, therefore, must be better policy”. World.title: The two factors that cut $450 from your household’s monthly budget
World.content:
Exclusive BusinessThe economySpending The two factors that cut $450 from your household’s monthly budget Matt Wade July 25, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Soaring petrol prices and multiple interest rate hikes have delivered the biggest quarterly hit to household finances in more than two decades. The spending power of families with a mortgage and two cars was slashed by an average of $450 per month in the March quarter this year, while non-essential funds available to a typical renter couple fell by $180 per month. Households that own their home outright were the least affected, with a drop in non-essential funds of $140 a month. Households have faced the steepest hit to their budgets in over two decades. Louie Douvis A report that tracks household finances by economic consultancy Polis Partners shows the first three months of 2026 saw the sharpest quarterly fall in discretionary household income since the series began in 2004. During that period, the Reserve Bank lifted interest rates twice and petrol prices surged above $2.50 a litre following attacks by the US and Israel on Iran in late February.



That financial double blow erased almost all the recovery that the average household made to their budgets over 2024 and 2025, leaving them “back where they were 15 years ago in real terms”, the study said. The Reserve Bank also lifted interest in May, but the effects of that decision were not included in the study. Polis Partners director Rob Tyson said this year has shown how quickly household budgets can deteriorate when multiple cost pressures arrive at the same time. “There’s been a big jump in what households have to devote to essentials and that leaves an awful lot less to spend on other things,” he said.



But the impact has been uneven. “Housing circumstances, household composition and income all shape how exposed a family is,” Tyson said. “A couple with a mortgage and two petrol cars they rely on to run the kids around and commute to work were really hit hard, whereas a self-funded retiree couple who have paid off the house and drive an EV have been largely insulated from the shock.” The lowest 20 per cent of income earners have been disproportionately affected; for those households essential costs exceed income by about $81 a week on average, meaning they must draw on saving or use credit to make ends meet.



Households with middle and lower-middle incomes have seen a significant fall in the amount of discretionary funds available to spend. But high-income households, especially those who own their homes outright, have been relatively insulated from the cost-of-living squeeze. Over the whole year to March 2026, the amount the average household had to spend on non-essential items fell by $782. Tyson warns there may be more pain in sight for Australian households. “Unfortunately, the squeeze isn’t over,” he said.

World.title: Bulldogs close gap on top eight after upsetting Warriors
World.content:
Another gutsy win for Canterbury tonight, winning 18-6 after starting underdogs against a quality team.

The Bulldogs’ built their strong 2025 campaign on defence and they have shown more of that in the past fortnight, conceding just one try across two games, and had some quality flashes of attack as well tonight, particularly from back-rowers Viliame Kikau and Jacob Preston.

The result means the Bulldogs leapfrog the Raiders and Sea Eagles to move to ninth on the ladder, level on competition points with North Queensland who take on the Broncos tonight.

They have a tricky run home – Melbourne are next, then the Roosters, Rabbitohs, Dragons, Panthers and Broncos – but momentum counts for a lot in the NRL and Canterbury have got it at the moment.

Full-time: Bulldogs win 18-6 at Accor Stadium

World.title: There’s more than mythology to Australia’s most hyped new rock band
World.content:
CultureMusicReview There’s more than mythology to Australia’s most hyped new rock band Jules LeFevre and and Robert Moran July 25, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Swapmeet, Mount Zero ★★★ Mount Zero by Swapmeet: a remarkably focused debut. “Mount Zero is a place you pass but never go,” Swapmeet’s Maxwell Elphick says of the mountain that looms as the northernmost point of the Grampians. The band would pass by the cryptically named mountain again and again while journeying from their hometown of Adelaide to Melbourne to play gigs.



These long, empty road trips have become part of the much-hyped indie rock group’s mythology – their first-ever show in Wollongong was packed full of devoted Adelaideans who’d made the trip across the border in support. It’s appropriate, then, that their debut album stretches and turns like one of these trips. There’s the propulsive thud of single and opener I Know!, the messy dirge of Seeds and the breeziness of standout Sand, while smatterings of horns and shrieking guitars slap exclamation marks on Personal (Don’t Take it) and Halfway. Local breakout indie-rockers Swapmeet. Josh Sabini Band members Maxwell Elphick, Venus O’Broin, Jack Medlyn and Josh Doherty swap instruments and vocals throughout the album, which they pieced together in a Port Noarlunga pad that had a ping-pong table overlooking the ocean. Despite the musical chairs, Mount Zero is a remarkably focused and even debut album, with its icy atmosphere recalling ’90s alt-rock – and a solitary drive on an empty highway. Jules LeFevre



Frost Children, Tweaker Poem ★★★★ Tweaker Poem by Frost Children: anthemic EDM at its serrated best. NYC-via-Midwest sibling duo Lulu and Angel Prost have seen their star rise exponentially since last year’s Sister, their sixth album in as many years, and their production work with the likes of Kim Petras and Ninajirachi. With that increasing profile has come a major label record deal and unwanted attention of the parasocial kind. Following an encounter with an overzealous fan (the EP’s eponymous “tweaker”), the duo fled New York and decamped to Tokyo, where – jet-lagged and sleep-deprived – they recorded this EP inspired by the entire ordeal. In songs that quote Madonna’s stalker Robert Dewey Hoskins and Rhonda Saunders’ book Whisper of Fear: the True Story of the Prosecutor Who Stalks the Stalkers, the pair scrutinise the encounter with emotional detail.



The result, somehow, isn’t dark or dour but life-affirming and warm, veering away from the brash indie sleaze they’re known for and further towards the pop aspirations and melodic melancholy that marked the best parts of Sister. Sibling duo Lulu and Angel Prost are Frost Children. Satellites and Light Leak match their hyperpop experimentalism with the sort of chart-topping emo-EDM that poured out of dorm rooms in the mid-2010s (think the Chainsmokers, Zedd, et al.), while the sparkling synths and serrated choruses of Creep and Afterlife lie somewhere between Dance Dance Revolution and Midwest emo. You’ll find yourself euphorically chanting “We never die, ain’t no cyanide!” over a frantic gabber beat like it’s a mantra. Robert Moran To read more from Spectrum, visit our page here. World.title: ‘Terrifying attack’: Accused rapist allegedly ambushed woman working from home
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts ‘Terrifying attack’: Accused rapist allegedly ambushed woman working from home Eleanor Campbell July 25, 2026 — 6:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A man accused of forcing himself into a woman’s home and threatening her with a knife before raping her on a kitchen floor has denied a string of sexual assaults in Melbourne’s outer west, including another case at a nearby school the following day. Timothy Richards, 39, appeared in Melbourne Magistrates Court on Saturday after being charged with two counts of rape, one count of aggravated burglary and one count of threats to kill. Police outside the scene of one of the alleged sexual assaults in Hoppers Crossing. Nine News Police allege he knocked on the door of a house on Whitsunday Drive, in Hoppers Crossing, on Thursday while the woman was alone and working from home. The court heard he had been living at an ex-partner’s house nearby and had approached the property 20 minutes earlier where the pair had engaged in a brief conversation.



Richards then allegedly produced a large kitchen knife and threatened to kill the 35-year-old woman before ordering her to remove her clothes as she screamed and pleaded with him to leave. The court heard the man, who police say was wearing a hoodie and had his face covered to conceal his identity, refused and grabbed her jacket, before dragging the woman into a nearby kitchen and sexually assaulting her. Loading It is alleged he then pushed the woman to the ground and raped her before getting up and walking out the front door. The woman told investigators she eventually got up and locked the door and called her husband when she realised he had left.



Sexual crimes squad detective Aiden Verdun described the alleged assault as a “terrifying attack on a vulnerable victim in the safety of her own home”. Richards has also been accused of another alleged sexual assault on Friday, when a woman was approached outside Mossfiel Primary School, in Langridge Street, Hoppers Crossing, about 6.45am. Police allege the woman, who was a staff member, was outside collecting bins when a man wearing a high-vis vest attempted to engage in a conversation with her before following her into a nearby classroom. The court heard the man placed the woman in a headlock as she fought and attempted to kick him off before he allegedly raped her. Detectives are also investigating a third incident where a 21-year-old woman was followed and grabbed at a nearby bus stop.



The woman recalled the man as being about six feet tall and of South-East Asian appearance. Investigators are trying to establish through DNA testing if the Hoppers Crossing incidents are linked. Richards, who denies all the allegations against him, was arrested on Friday morning. The court heard he was on bail for three separate matters, including charges of unlawful assault, assault with a weapon, criminal damage, and possession of methamphetamine. He appeared during a court hearing on Saturday afternoon with his shaved head down.



He will be remanded in custody and appear before a court on November 27. Police also attended a house in nearby Branton Road in Hoppers Crossing after a resident reported a possible burglary overnight Friday. The 39-year-old man will return to Melbourne Magistrates Court in October. With Ashleigh McMillan

World.title: Questions asked after monsoon-like rains sweep Wellington
World.content:
Questions are being raised about the cause of flooding in parts of the capital.

Wellington residents reported torrents surging down Tinakori Road in Thorndon on Saturday morning and rising around parked cars, with some joking a boat or kayak lane was needed on the busy street.

MetService issued a Severe Thunderstorm Warning for Wellington for the morning, including for torrential rain, after thunderstorms were detected near the city and airport, moving east-northeast. The formal alert was extended during the morning, before later being lifted.

Wellingtonian Rebekah Ward described watching floodwaters rising towards the doors of shops in Tinakori Road, while having breakfast there.

She said the "river" of water rose to the bottom of parked cars and even knocked over a scooter, prompting fears her own vehicle could be swept away.

The timing of the downpour was an "ironic" reminder of the monsoon she would soon experience on a trip to India, Ward said.

"There were cars parked along Tinakori Road and the water was getting higher and higher and higher... and I could see that the water was getting up to the level of the bottom of the car door, and I was thinking 'oh gosh, am I going to have a car when this is finished?'

MetService meteorologist Paris Marshall said multiple reports and observations of hail and intense rainfall were logged across the capital on Saturday morning as the storm moved east toward Lower Hutt.

The intensity was at a level where flash flooding around streams, gullies and urban areas were possible, and instruments recorded 40 millimetres of rain in half an hour at MetService's Kelburn station, near Tinakori Road, Marshall said.

Fire and Emergency NZ said it had no weather-related callouts from the downpours.

Responding to commentary on social media, Wellington's deputy mayor Ben McNulty said three-water provider Tiaki Wai should investigate what went wrong, adding that the area had not flooded significantly during heavy rain events earlier in the year.

Tiaki Wai was approached for comment.

However, Tiaki Wai did issue an alert that heavy rain had lead to a discharge of fully treated wastewater into the Waiwhetū Stream, in Lower Hutt, which empties into Wellington Harbour.

This could make the water discharge appear cloudy or murky or mean it has an odour, they warned, and all recreational water users should follow Land Air Water Aotearoa (LAWA) advice and stay out of the stream the next two to three days.

The LAWA website had all swimming spots on the north and east of Wellington Harbour as well as Oriental Bay marked as unsuitable for swimming, on Saturday.

Snowfall warnings issued for high parts of the country, strong wind watch for Auckland

Elsewhere in the country, MetService issued snowfall warnings for the Desert Road (SH1) and Lewis Pass (SH7), while strong southwest winds prompted a yellow Strong Wind Watch for Auckland, through till 7pm Saturday.

Snow was expected to settle on Desert Road from late Saturday afternoon and into the evening, with 2 to 4cm possible near the summit and light flurries down to 800m.

World.title: How learning te reo Māori in her 70's transformed one Pākehā grandmother's view of Aotearoa
World.content:
"Open your heart."

Those are the kupu one Pākehā grandmother hopes will encourage more New Zealanders to take their first step toward te reo Māori and te ao Māori.

Gael Finlayson-Davis, grandmother of six and great-grandmother of two, now in her 70s, became an unexpected symbol of this year's Matariki celebrations after speaking through tears at the national hautapu ceremony at Takaparawhau.

Her emotional kōrero, in which she described learning te reo Māori as part of her hope for "a better future for our country", resonated with thousands.

Although learning te reo is something she wishes she had embraced decades earlier, she hopes her story shows it is never too late.

"If I can do it in my 70s, anyone can," she told RNZ.

"Open your heart. Just listen and learn. There is so much generosity in the Māori community that if you take a step forward, you will be met."

Even learning basic greetings and taking the time to pronounce Māori place names correctly, she believes, is an act of respect.

"You would do that in countries overseas, so why would you not try in your own country?"

Finlayson-Davis was a probation officer and later a clinical psychologist. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

Raised on a farm near Dargaville, Finlayson-Davis describes her childhood as a typical rural upbringing of the 1950s and 60s, surrounded by whānau and generations living side by side.

Although there were few Māori at her school, one experience stayed with her for decades.

"I remember going on a marae visit when I was about 12, and I remember just being blown away and thinking there's something here that I feel very drawn to. I didn't understand it and I didn't know how to access it, but it was an important experience in my young life."

That feeling never disappeared.

Throughout her career as a probation officer and later as a clinical psychologist, she worked alongside many Māori. Witnessing the inequities many of her clients faced only deepened her desire to better understand te ao Māori, she said.

"I saw so many young Māori offenders who'd had a very tough time in their lives, often through children's homes and borstal. It seemed like things could have been very different for them if they'd had different opportunities, and that really affected me."

She enrolled in her first te reo Māori class while in her 30s, but raising two daughters, building a career and family life meant the language had to take a back seat.

Only after retiring did she finally return to learning through Selwyn Community Education.

"It's been really hard. I'm not a natural linguist and I will never be fluent, but I've learnt such a lot, such a tremendous amount. As a person very interested in language, written language and meaning, I love the whakataukī and the waiata and the significance for different iwi, so it has unlocked something important for me as a Pākehā that I would not have had otherwise."

RNZ / Richard Tindiller

Learning te reo became a way of understanding Aotearoa differently, she said.

"Though it will never be my language or my culture, by learning the reo you unlock so much about the culture that you're unaware of if you don't speak the reo."

"Māori have such a beautiful way of honouring the natural world, the whenua, the awa and the moana. I just really appreciate all of that."

One of the greatest lessons, she said, was recognising that her experience of learning te reo as a Pākehā is fundamentally different from the experience of Māori reclaiming their own language.

"I'm very aware that for a Pākehā to learn te reo and for a Māori to learn te reo, they're two extremely different experiences."

"The anguish of Māori who are having to reclaim their own language rather than being brought up with it and being fluent in it... I feel very humbled by the effort that that takes and the emotional toll it takes."

"Whereas for me it's quite different. I come with curiosity and an openness, but I don't have that emotional anguish that I'm reclaiming something I should never have lost."

She said learning more about Aotearoa's history had also been confronting.

"Yes, it is confronting. It is. And it's confronting in a way that needs to be experienced."

While Finlayson-Davis said while Aotearoa has come a long way, she believes there is still work to do.

"I have been very disturbed by recent attempts to remove the reo, and aspects of Māori representation on councils, and I find that disheartening... we've struggled hard to get to this point, which is some way, but to see that being dismantled has been heartbreaking actually.

"Clearly there are people who feel antagonistic towards Māori and I don't really understand it, because we have a partnership, and to honour that would make us very strong.

"We could do better than we're doing at the moment."

Aucklander Gael Finlayson-Davis was one of the many Pākehā New Zealanders watching this year's Matariki hautapu ceremony at Bastion Point - she said it was a beautiful and emotional experience. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

She said too often people viewed Māori success as coming at someone else's expense.

"People seem to think that if Māori thrive, then Pākehā will suffer."

"No. Māori don't want to make a country that's better just for Māori. They want to make a country that's better for everyone. That would be taking care of climate and whenua and waterways and people, so everyone would thrive."

She points to the way marae respond during times of crisis as an example of the country Aotearoa could be.

"We only need to look at what happens in a crisis, and marae open and manaakitanga is extended to anyone who turns up. That's a strength in our community."

"We could be so much better with both Pākehā and Māori working collaboratively rather than in some sort of contest, as if [when] someone gets something it's taking away from someone else. No. We're adding to it for everyone."

Finlayson-Davis said she is not alone in this way of thinking, and said there are many others like her embracing Māori culture. She attends a waiata Māori kaupapa every Monday, where she says up to 20 Pākehā wāhine attend each week.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/te-ao-maori/532750/the-pakeha-project-a-tangata-tiriti-led-push-for-tino-rangatiratanga

"I don't consider myself unusual in thinking that there are many Pākehā who are well disposed towards Māori being fully represented and acknowledged within our nation in ways that are appropriate to them, and that seems to me that could make us a special country."

As a grandmother and great-grandmother, she said she feels hopeful seeing younger generations learning te reo Māori, tikanga and waiata from their earliest years at school.

World.title: ACT wants hunters in charge of game animals on conservation land, not DOC
World.content:
The ACT party wants to give hunters a "real stake in managing and looking after our conservation estate".

The party wants to transfer the responsibility for game animals on conservation land from the Department of Conservation (DOC) to the Game Animal Council.

ACT's spokesperson for conservation, Cameron Luxton, said the party's policy for hunters is about recognising them as the "conservationists they are".

The party would also recognise game animal and game-bird species as "natural resources to be sustainably managed" in legislation, and designate certain game herds, such as Stewart Island whitetail deer, as "Herds of Special Interest".

The party would reward hunters for verified conservation outcomes, improve hunting access to public land and protect lawful hunting by creating infringement offences for interfering with hunts. Interference could include the use of drones and helicopters.

ACT deputy leader Nicole McKee announced the policy at the Hunting & Wildlife Expo on the weekend.

Speaking to RNZ, Luxton said giving hunters a "real voice" in managing the conservation estate was "well overdue".

He explained the Game Animal Council was established in 2013, with the purpose of being a voice for hunters and to be involved in decisions around game animals.

But ACT wants the council to be empowered beyond just consultation, and to be funded by the money currently available to DOC for managing these animals.

"It's time government stopped getting in hunters' way and started trusting them with the responsibility they've earned."

Luxton said that DOC could not manage the country's estate alone, adding that hunting groups were already providing hundreds of hours towards conservation efforts, "looking after tracks, maintenance on huts, and importantly predator control".

He said introduced species became pests when unmanaged, but also held deep value to New Zealanders, be it "cultural value, historic value, and even meat value for the table".

"Any virtue taken too far becomes a vice, but managing our valued species is incredibly important."

He used deer that were already in the conservation estate as an example, and the ability for hunters to manage them in a way that made sense for communities that utilised them, but also for the environment they lived in.

"Hunters aren't out there trying to do damage to the environment.

World.title: Christchurch landlords ordered to pay $400 for broken water feature
World.content:
When Shuo Chang and Min Wu moved into their rental, they expected to enjoy the view of two water features outside their window.

Instead, they were "denied the pleasure" of one water feature and had to look out at a giant urn-like feature that was bone dry because their landlords could not get it to work.

Now Christchurch landlords Lisa Smart and Jeremy Smart, as trustees of the Smart Family Trust, must pay Chang and Wu $400 in compensation for the non-working feature after the tenants took their case to the Tenancy Tribunal.

Chang told Open Justice that the case was never just about a fountain.

"We moved into a home with existing defects, spent two years reporting recurring maintenance problems, and then faced claims seeking to make us pay for the property's wear and repair costs," Chang claimed.

"When we reported water ingress, it was not treated as urgent; after we left, the same issue became the basis of claims totalling $14,000. Those claims were dismissed, but we left the tribunal feeling that we had not been heard on equal terms."

He said both he and the landlords were appealing the decision.

Both the tenants and landlords had applied to the tribunal regarding several issues during the now-ended two-year tenancy.

The tenants sought compensation and exemplary damages for various alleged breaches of the landlords' obligations and repayment of the bond, while the landlords sought compensation for the tenants' alleged failure to allow proper access to the premises and for loss and expense relating to their attendance at the hearing.

Tribunal adjudicator Ross Armstrong said in his recently released decision that there were two water features in the garden of the property.

When the tenancy began, one worked and one did not.

The one that did not work was black and shaped like an urn. When filled with water and working, the water overflowed and cascaded down its exterior, where it was collected and recirculated.

The landlords were unable to get it to work during the tenancy.

The tenants told the tribunal the property manager had told them before the tenancy began that both water features worked.

"They say that they have been denied the pleasure of looking out the kitchen window and seeing the water spilling out of the urn and running down its surface," Armstrong said.

He accepted the tenants were entitled to have two working water features, and as they were part of the premises, the landlords were required to provide and maintain them in a reasonable state of repair.

"From my assessment of the messages relating to the water feature, I accept that the tenants wanted it to work. I also accept that they would have taken pleasure from seeing it working when they were looking out the kitchen window or when they were out enjoying the garden.

"In my view, I must assess the value of the loss of a working water feature based on how it would affect the average person. That is a person who is not indifferent to it or one who is especially enamoured by it.

"It is a small part of what comprises the amenity and enjoyment of the premises, but some compensation is warranted."

He ruled $400 was appropriate.

The tenants also applied for compensation for claims regarding flickering lights, a heat pump that they said was faulty, an alleged mice infestation, a broken garage door, a leak in the ensuite, a breach of quiet enjoyment and having to do garden work they deemed "forced labour".

In his decision, Armstrong said there was a lack of evidence to support those claims and they could not be proved.

Landlord's claims also dismissed

The landlords applied for compensation regarding the ensuite leak, claiming the tenants prevented them from completing repairs until after they moved out.

The tenants notified the landlord of the leak and insisted that only the landlords' qualified contractor could attend to investigate the situation and limited the visit to 30 minutes.

The landlords' builder attended and subsequently reported that there was unlikely to be a leak, and if there was, there was no urgency to deal with it. The landlords left it until after the tenants had vacated.

They then fixed the problem, including regrouting the shower and ensuite floor with waterproof grout.

The landlords claimed $4000 for the cost of the work and $10,000 in lost rent, saying the tenants had delayed the work by asserting they would not allow it to be done while they were living in the property.

Armstrong dismissed the claim, finding that the tenants had correctly reported the apparent leak and that the landlords had decided to leave the work until after the tenancy ended because it was considered non-urgent.

The landlords also claimed losses and expenses arising from the litigation, but the claim was denied.

Armstrong also ordered the tenants' $4000 bond be refunded.

It was not the first time this tenancy had ended up before the tribunal. In early 2025, the landlords claimed compensation for damage to a kitchen worktop and a contribution towards the cost of an electrician replacing lights.

The tenants claimed compensation for interference with their quiet enjoyment and for a breach of the landlords' maintenance obligations.

The tenants' claims included allegations that the lights in the premises flickered and at times failed to work altogether, and that a water feature did not function, issues that were also raised in the latest application.

At the time, all claims were dismissed.

Armstrong was able to consider the claims regarding the faulty lights and non-working water feature but only for the period ending with the previous hearing on 27 January, 2025.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Civil Defence website crash during tsunami alert due to third-party problems - minister
World.content:
The Emergency Management Minister has been told problems with third party services crashed the Civil Defence website during a tsunami alert.

And work is underway to speed up an emergency map system that was too slow.

The website went down during last week's Fiordland earthquake and tsunami event.

Mark Mitchell met with the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) on Tuesday.

He said it told him it had extensively strength-tested the website over the last year.

"But issues with third party services led to Thursday's outage."

This was an "unfortunate combination" of a problem with the firewall - that has since been fixed - and a global outage affecting the software controlling the failover to NEMA's backup site.

NEMA was working with the third party responsible for the failover software and had put in place manual processes meantime to function in an emergency.

"I have instructed NEMA officials to provide me with regular reporting as permanent fixes are progressed," Mitchell said in a statement.

A second piece of emergency tech also failed to perform as it should, both in the tsunami alert and in the earlier Wairoa evacuation alert, when the new emergency mobile alert map did not update as quickly as it should.

"The current feed is proving too slow for live alerts, and NEMA is now redesigning how the map handles the data behind the scenes so it can refresh more regularly," Mitchell told RNZ.

Text alerts went to residents in both events, and the map is mostly for media or friends and family outside the area to know where alerts apply to.

It was still in the testing phase. "These recent events have been valuable in helping NEMA to identify improvements," the minister said.

World.title: Live: Youngster hurt as Dons cop belting from Hawks, Swans dominate Giants
World.content:
Jack Gunston kicked seven goals as Hawthorn recorded a 93-point win over Essendon. (Getty Images)

Evergreen veteran Jack Gunston has kicked seven goals, including his 600th AFL major, to lead Hawthorn to a thumping 93-point win over Essendon.

Fresh off signing a one-year contract extension to take him into an 18th season, the magnificent Gunston, 34, headlined a 19.18 (132) to 5.9 (39) smashing that tightened Hawthorn's grip on a top-four berth.

Essendon defender Jordan Ridley was forced out in the second quarter with a foot injury — and Gunston put undersized defender Mason Redman to the sword.

The three-time premiership forward booted three goals in the second term then four in the third, with the MCG crowd of 42,509 erupting when he nailed his sixth goal for his 600th league major.

Gunston also became the VFL/AFL's 37th greatest goalkicker and surpassed former teammate Luke Breust as Hawthorn's seventh all-time greatest goal kicker.

Essendon was initially buoyed by its drought-breaking win over GWS last week, but Sam Mitchell's Hawthorn — who still hope to add Suns spearhead Ben King to their loaded attack — broke away with six unanswered goals in the second quarter.

Midfielders Will Day (21 disposals, two goals), Jai Newcombe (28 disposals) and Josh Ward (32 disposals) and half-back Jarman Impey (37 disposals) were influential while Nick Watson jagged three goals.

Essendon had few winners around the ground, with Nate Caddy fighting his way to three goals.

Essendon lost youngster Sullivan Robey to a knee injury in the third quarter. (Getty Images)

Zach Merrett, who was desperate to get to Hawthorn last year and is expected to seek a trade again, was Essendon's leading disposal winner with 21 touches plus nine tackles.

It was a horror day of injuries for second-last Essendon, currently in its head coach recruiting process, and interim boss Dean Solomon.

Injury-plagued Ridley, also expected to seek a trade at season's end came off, while young gun Sullivan Robey was helped off with a right knee injury suffered in a tackle early in the third term.

The Bombers were hopeful Robey had only suffered a knee knock.

Archer Day-Wicks (right hip) limped off at the start of the final quarter.

Hawthorn's day was soured by a first-quarter concussion to Mitch Lewis, who ran into the back of Day-Wicks when laying a tackle and clashed heads with the Bomber.

A dazed Lewis, who had blood streaming from his right eyebrow, received treatment and at one point dropped to one knee but was able to walk off.

Lewis, fresh off signing a four-year contract extension, will miss next Saturday's clash with North Melbourne in Tasmania.

Essendon dug in initially but Gunston nabbed two goals in quick succession to set Hawthorn on their way early in the second quarter.

The Hawks never looked back from there, leading by 45 at halftime, then 74 at three-quarter time before kicking away again for their third straight win.

The Bombers host Adelaide at Docklands Stadium next Sunday.

AAP

World.title: 'Blight on the sport': Fight cancelled on Tszyu card after weigh-in
World.content:
Luckless Australian boxer Liam Wilson has been dealt another cruel blow, with his scheduled world title eliminator against Stephen Fulton cancelled after the American failed to make weight.

In farcical scenes, Fulton hit the scales at almost 63.5kg on Saturday, almost 4.5kg more than the two-division world champion was originally supposed to fight Wilson at in Sydney.

Fulton and Wilson were supposed to square off at the super-featherweight of 59kg before officials on Friday raised the weight to 60.3kg for the feature bout on the blockbuster Tim Tszyu-Errol Spence Jr card.

Wilson had happily agreed to the late change, saying he was desperate to earn another world title shot with a victory over the former unified super-bantamweight world champion and ex-WBC featherweight belt holder.

But now the American's team is being accused of never truly intending to fight on Sunday.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"This feels like a stitch-up," Wilson's manager and Tszyu's ex-agent Glenn Jennings said.

"If you are serious and you sign a contract at 133 [pounds], there is an expectation that you will deliver.

"It is not only unacceptable, it is a blight on the sport. This is unprofessional, there is nowhere to go for this bloke now."

Undefeated Olympian Paulo Aokuso will move to the main card, taking on Luis Tejeda from the Dominican Republic in a light-heavyweight bout.

Wilson's fight is the second co-main event to be cancelled this week after Fulton's fellow American Jermall Charlo was denied a visa to face rising Australian Koen Mazoudier.

World.title: 'We can all feel it': Bronze medal lifts Aussie gymnasts' outlook
World.content:
Australian gymnast Jesse Moore had a sinking feeling in his stomach: he had seen this movie before.

Four years ago at the Commonwealth Games in Birmingham, the nation's best male artistic gymnasts fell agonisingly short of bronze by 0.650 points after slipping at the death to Cyprus.

Fast forward to Glasgow and Australia found themselves in a similar position when hosts Scotland mounted a late challenge en route to the final of six apparatuses.

With just one point the difference in the men's final at Glasgow International Stadium, Australia's five-man squad withstood the raucous home crowd and proved their mettle on the pommel horse to avoid history repeating.

Bolstered by a strong start on rings and horizontal bar, Australia clinched bronze with a combined score of 235.650 points.

A near-flawless Canada team won gold (241.400 points), pipping 2022 Birmingham champions England by 3.150 points.

Australia's men won their first team medal since their maiden gold at the 2010 Delhi Games, doing so with four debutants in the five-man squad.

Paris Olympian Moore was the only Australian man to have experience on the Games stage, leading Ritam Malik, James Hardy, Ben Foster and Tru Hagens.

Australia's Ritam Malik flips through the air after performing on the rings. (Getty Images: Jane Barlow/PA Images)

Moore, 23, laughed when asked if his mind went back to the 2022 Games.

"You always have that in the back of your mind," Moore said.

"But we have got a job to do. The game's not over yet.

"The way we finished on pommel is pretty extraordinary. It shows how well we've come over the past few years.

"It's a bit weird being one of the oldest and most experienced on the team. I'm proud to be that in this team.

"We're certainly on track, only upwards from here.

"We can all feel it and people back home can feel it as well."

Moore notched Australia's second-best score (13.300) on the apparatus behind Malik (13.500), while 19-year-old Hagens was awarded 13.100 points despite falling.

Pommel horse specialist Hagens had waited through the nearly four-hour final for his only apparatus.

Australia claims six gold on Commonwealth Games opening day Australia claims six gold medals, and 13 overall, to open competition on day one of the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Hagens started his 40-second cameo just as Scotland began their last-ditch effort for the podium on the horizontal bar.

Cameron Lynn (13.500) and Reuben Ward (13.150) matched it with the Australians, but crowd favourite Hamish Carter scored 12.900 points.

"I was pretty nervous," Hagens said.

"Not the outcome I wanted, but it was good to get up there, finish it off for the team, to get up a score we needed to get the medal."

A horrific injury to English gymnast Gabriel Langton put a damper on the final.

Langton had to be stretchered from the Glasgow International Arena after falling from the horizontal bar and landing on his head and neck, resulting in a 15-minute pause in competition.

The 19-year-old lay motionless on the ground for several minutes, but gave a thumbs up as he left the arena.

World.title: Waratahs defeat Drua to claim seventh Super Rugby Women's title
World.content:
The NSW Waratahs have won their seventh Super Rugby Women's championship with a comprehensive 34-17 victory over the Fijian Drua in Ba.

The Waratahs claimed a third straight title after dominating the Drua, who had finished the regular season on top of the standings.

Leading 24-0 during the second half, the Waratahs were always in command, running in six tries to three for the match.

Reserve winger Amelia Whitaker touched down for a double, while Maya Stewart, Desiree Miller, Faliki Pohiva and Rosie Ferguson also crossed the stripe.

Maya Stewart was among the Waratahs' try scorers in the grand final. (Getty Images: Pita Simpson)

Miller landed two conversions for the victors.

Pohiva produced a barnstorming performance and was deservedly named player of the match.

Nunia Daunimoala managed a brace of tries for the Drua, and Sulita Waisega scored a consolation five-pointer just seconds before the full-time siren sounded.

The Waratahs had lost their final two matches of the regular season but rebounded to comfortably win their semifinal against the Western Force in Perth, 33-22.

The Drua's only defeats came against the Waratahs, who had won 42-29 when the two teams met in Sydney in round one.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: LeBron's new teammates go wild as NBA star announces move
World.content:
LeBron James's first "final" decision was that he would retire.

Weeks of deep reflection led him to change his mind, however, with all the familiar options in front of him to extend his career; a third trip with Cleveland, a second stop in Miami, maybe even stay in California for a high-profile union in Golden State.

But it was nope to all of those teams.

The blaring headline in bold letters still seemed like a feverish dream to the bulk of a fan base who was not even alive the last time the franchise won a title, but it is true: LeBron James is heading to the Philadelphia 76ers.

Loading Instagram content

The NBA's all-time leading scorer made the announcement on social media overnight, saying it will be his "last decision" and that it comes after he strongly considered retirement.

"I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team and I am so excited to energise a new fan base and start this incredible journey one last time," James said.

A four-time NBA champion, James wrote he was "done" when his 23rd NBA season ended and that it was his last with the Los Angeles Lakers.

"I was pretty sure I played my last game. I was honest at that last press conference when I said I needed to look at myself and decide if I still love this game," James wrote.

"I still truly love this game, and I have more to give."

The 41-year-old James is set to sign a modest $US8 million ($11.4 million), two-year contract on the veteran minimum salary with the Sixers, according to ESPN. He made nearly $53 million last season.

"I'm not going for money. I'm not going for family," James wrote.

"What am I really playing for at this point? I still want to sacrifice. I still want to work. I still want to grind. I still want to compete, to win and to have a chance at the feeling of winning."

James celebrated his decision on Instagram with a career highlight reel set to Philadelphia rapper Meek Mill's Dreams and Nightmares, the adopted sports anthem of city teams.

LeBron James left the Los Angeles Lakers, with rumours connecting him to Miami, Cleveland, or another team in LA. (Getty Images: Harry How)

The video ends with the lyric, "hold up, wait a minute. Y'all thought I was finished?" and cuts to a 76ers' logo.

Sportswear company Fanatics already had his number 23 jersey on sale for $125 with delivery not expected until the end of August. The company sold out within hours of the announcement.

Much as James did for Cleveland when he ended a 56-year championship drought for the city by leading the Cavaliers to the title in 2016, he can snap a lengthy title drought for the Sixers.

The Sixers went 45-37 last season and were swept in the second round by the NBA champion New York Knicks.

Most betting sites had the Sixers as 9-1 favourites to win the championship behind the Oklahoma City Thunder, the San Antonio Spurs and the New York Knicks, as of Saturday morning.

James joins a 76ers team that has not won an NBA championship since 1983 and has not advanced out of the second round of the Eastern Conference play-offs since 2001.

Philadelphia star Tyrese Maxey reacts to the news LeBron James is joining the team. (Instagram: @tyresemaxey)

The 76ers should boast one of the top starting fives in the NBA with second-year standout VJ Edgecombe, fellow All-Stars Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown — the 2024 NBA Finals MVP, a five-time All-Star and the league's fourth-leading scorer this past season acquired in a stunning off-season deal with the Celtics.

Maxey posted an Instagram story of him celebrating in a gym and yelling "What? What!" over the news while Brown wrote on X "#throwtheballup."

Brown wrote the same phrase in his introductory note to Philadelphia, and it has already been branded on billboards throughout the city.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro even proclaimed Friday as LeBron James Day in the state.
